speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Like what Minister Lawrence Wong said yesterday, many in the food and beverage (F&B) and wholesale trade sectors felt a lot more struggling this time round; more shaken as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Businesses and the public at large have expected restrictions to be further relaxed as we approach the major milestone where at least two-thirds of our population will be fully vaccinated in August.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It was not to be, following the outbreaks at KTV lounges and the Jurong Fishery Port.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Those in the F&B and retail sectors find this series of roller coaster measures disruptive and added stresses to their already dire finances and also their operations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Those supporting the F&B sectors are also feeling the knock-on effects as they saw a sudden drop in their orders.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These latest heightened measures happened despite the country reaching a higher vaccination rate among our population of now greater than 50%, better testing capacity, enhanced contact tracing capabilities and our healthcare system not under significant stress.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Which is why the F&B operators who had hoped for more calibrated measures such as limiting dining-in to those who are fully vaccinated and backed by the rapid ring-fencing capabilities that we now have.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But I am heartened that the Finance Minister and the MTI Minister have heard the concerns raised by the F&B businesses and taking in their feedback.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Of course, businesses would prefer to have their top line back again, that is, have their businesses and sales back again to earn their keeps.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These are the companies that support the F&B and retail sector, such as the wholesale trades, logistics, distributors and suppliers to the F&B sector.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They felt neglected in the latest round of support measures like the JSS and the rental reduction assistance.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They suffered from both supply-side and demand-side pressures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, on the supply side, the cost of storage spaces has not come down while air and sea freight costs have risen.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: On the demand side, the temporary stoppage of dining-in has significantly reduced orders.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These businesses also hire a high number of Singaporean workers and many are already on a four-day work week.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These supporting sectors function in tandem with the F&B businesses and whenever the F&B sector enter a lockdown, they are also directly impacted.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: With tightened safe management measures, many events and activities are either cancelled, postponed or downsized.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Corporate MICE events, community events, schools' regular events, graduations, weddings, anniversary celebrations have all either swung into virtual format or are simply cancelled.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In my constituency, I have had to cancel some events due to the heightened measures as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many of the event companies are quality local talents capable of hosting world-class events.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: What they need are both a minimum base load of activities as well as some support measures from the Government to keep going and to preserve their capabilities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It gave the businesses a good level of confidence and some predictability as to how to plan ahead and how to live with endemic COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As was alluded to in yesterday's Ministerial Statement by Minister Lawrence Wong, even with a high vaccination rate among our population, we can still expect occasional sharp rises in cases due to new variants.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, when we resume business and leisure travels, we may, from time to time, experience imported infiltrations that can potentially lead to a big cluster.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Heightened measures may still be necessary from time to time even when we achieve herd immunity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: That has to be featured in the contingency planning for businesses going forward.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: If the situation is severe, such as where businesses and livelihoods are seriously affected, the Government may again need to step in with a fresh dosage of direct support measures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is something that businesses feel comforted about because the Government will always be there to help when we are faced with serious situations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: On the other hand, operating revenue remains uncertain as it really hinges on the state of the economy, which, in turn, depends on how the pandemic situation develops and how countries around the world respond to the crisis and whether they have stabilised their own domestic situations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I can imagine that the availability of such unutilised expenditures for reallocation would increasingly be fewer and it would increasingly be more challenging to squeeze out the next drop of additional funding from the reallocations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask the Minister for Finance if there are plans to review the entire development expenditures of the Government and whether we need to reprioritise the timeline, given the COVID-19 environment so as to free up more contingency funding?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I am sure this additional NIRC will be welcomed and helpful to the Minister for Finance as he juggles and balances a very delicate and challenging fiscal situation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I believe this is the largest NIRC ever – thanks to the steady good performance of our investment agencies and also to our prudent approach of accumulating and compounding the financial reserves over the decades.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Over the last one week or so, I was also happy to read reports of improved performances by Temasek Holdings and GIC amidst a more volatile global market environment.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Notwithstanding, we have to expect markets and asset valuations to constantly be fluctuating and, hence, this sound and prudent way of computing the NIRC by smoothing out the expected investment returns over a long period is necessary to ensure steady and predictable net investment returns contribution for the purpose of Budgets and cash flow planning.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: With more infrastructure assets being funded by SINGA in the years ahead, we can expect the Debt Servicing Costs to also rise over time, adding new variables to the equation in how we balance the annual Budgets.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We will spend more, for sure, whether for COVID-19 or to take care of the well-being of our people, whether it is for our security, economy, environment or necessarily to also invest in our future.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I cannot envisage a situation where we would spend less in the future.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Cutting costs to balance our Budget will increasingly not be a palatable option.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I am sure Members in this House will agree.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have to keep finding ways to grow our revenues and not lose sight of our core fundamentals that underpin economic growth, like always staying ahead of the curve, staying competitive and staying open.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: That is the only way we can build a Singapore that can last.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Minister said that, in the near future, COVID-19 cases could be dealt with very differently from now.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, an infected person who is vaccinated could be allowed to recover from home.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Subsequently, on 7 July, Minister Lawrence Wong revealed that gatherings in groups of eight might be allowed by the end of July when at least half the population would be fully vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The KTV cluster and the Jurong Fishery Port (JFP) outbreaks were the first major setback in our roadmap for reopening since its announcement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When the KTV cluster first swelled to 120 cases on 16 July, Minister Gan Kim Yong said that instead of rolling back COVID-19 measures like before, MOH will continue to take a targeted approach to protect the unvaccinated.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The vaccinated will be allowed to continue gathering in groups of five in mask-off settings while the unvaccinated could only gather in groups of two.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The targeted approach was abandoned, and F&B and gym operators had to face the same restrictions they had just only exited.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Essentially, just a year after we completed our circuit breaker in 2020, Singapore has snapped back twice into states of quasi-lockdown on almost all social and non-essential activities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Minister Ong explained in yesterday's Ministerial Statement that the KTV cluster alone would not have necessitated the roll-back to Phase Two (Heightened Alert).

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But when the JFP cluster started to grow, the MTF felt that it was necessary to take firmer measures to protect the elderly and the unvaccinated.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I understand the MTF's desire to err on the side of caution in this case.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, beyond this round of Phase Two (Heightened Alert), Singaporeans and businesses need more clarity on how the roadmap for reopening is going to be implemented.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: After 18 August, if more large clusters break out, will we need to brace ourselves for more rolling lockdowns?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many businesses, especially in the F&B, arts and sports sectors, are suffering not only because of the safe management measures (SMMs) but also because of the frequent changes in policies, which can actually hurt them even more.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The lack of certainty makes it difficult for business owners to decide if they should stay the course or pivot to a more pandemic-resilient line of business.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Individual workers, too, need to decide whether or not to continue hoping for more COVID-19 support grants or pivot their careers to a more stable line of work, if such options are available.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Not only are the policies sometimes changing overnight, but some of them are painfully complicated.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When the restrictions on the now-defunct Phase Three (Heightened Alert) from 19 July to 8 August were announced, some remarked that one needed a PhD to understand the dining-in rules.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Not only was there differentiation between the vaccinated and unvaccinated, children and adults, same family or different household, but there was also differentiation between the types of vaccines received, whether Sinovac or mRNA, and the number of doses that counts as fully vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Restaurant staff would find it challenging to enforce these rules with their patrons, some of whom may not have the TraceTogether app installed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some fast food outlets initially decided to simply adopt the strictest interpretation of all the rules for all patrons.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This benefits neither the industry nor its customers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: No one would disagree with a calibrated approach to SMMs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, the practicality of such measures was not evident in the recent attempt.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I hope the MTF will take on board lessons learned from the experience when formulating the rules as we look forward to some re-opening on 19 August and beyond.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Next, I would like to speak on how information on our battle with COVID-19 is presented.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The daily infection numbers have become a key focus for many people.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: MOH highlights these numbers in their daily updates and the media splashes it on the headlines.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans too mention these numbers in our conversations with one another.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Experts will tell us that new case counts alone are not an accurate gauge of whether things are going well in our fight against COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There are many other factors that need to be taken into account when deciding the level of risk we are facing.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet, most laymen are not capable of synthesising so much information at one go.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This index could weigh various factors including the vaccination rate, hospitalisation rate, positivity rate of testing, contact tracing efficiency, new infections per 100,000 people and the infection risk of other countries, among others.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will require some calculations and intelligent assumptions by experts to produce a single daily number that the public can more easily digest.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It should be a leading indicator, not a lagging one.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am not suggesting that the MTF should be bound by this risk index when deciding on policies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, the index can serve as a guide to both policymakers and the public to understand the current risk levels and adapt accordingly.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: An objective, science-based COVID-19 Risk Index will help assure the public that SMMs imposed by the Government are appropriate for the given risk levels.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This would secure more buy-in from the public and result in greater voluntary compliance with SMMs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Voluntary compliance is key in our battle against the virus, as demonstrated by the KTV cluster outbreak, which was most likely caused by a wilful disregard for social distancing regulations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: No amount of rules and fines will stop people from engaging in risky activities behind closed doors if they are not convinced of the risks.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There are not many countries around the world that have come up with a COVID-19 Risk Index which is both accurate and widely understood by the public.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore has an opportunity to lead the way in this respect.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Government can give consideration to this proposal.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I shall now move on to a related factor in our roadmap for reopening, which is vaccinations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: During my estate visits and house visits, I make it a point to ask residents, especially the elderly, if they have gotten their vaccinations and encourage those who have not to do so soon for their own protection.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Thankfully, most residents assure me that they have gotten their jabs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, I find vaccine hesitancy among a small minority of the population rather worrying.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Based on the reasons they articulate, it appears that a lot of their misunderstanding about vaccinations is fuelled by confusing information they receive from friends through private messaging platforms.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I myself receive a daily stream of such messages from friends and residents.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The situation is more complicated than just scientific arguments for or against vaccinations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have heard accusations of vaccine manufacturers colluding with governments to promote their vaccines; that the vaccines have not been fully approved and, therefore, are merely experimental; or that Singapore is biased against or towards vaccines from some countries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These have been circulating since the end of last year and have steadily increased in virulence and virality in the last few months.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Instead of politicians fronting the public education campaign for vaccinations, more can be done to amplify the voice of independent medical experts to explain the facts and allay the public's fears.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Other experts in business, international relations and culture also have a role to play in addressing misinformation about vaccines.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This must be done soon, before the window of opportunity to change minds closes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Once news about large COVID-19 clusters fades from the headlines, the impetus to get vaccinated will decrease.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have some questions about the latest COVID-19 support measures which I hope the Finance Minister can address.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, I note this is provided only to stallholders in Government hawker centres and markets.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, I would like to point out some implementation anomalies from the previous rounds of the grant.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have a resident who works as a dishwasher and was asked to go on no-pay leave while his foreign worker colleagues were not.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Apparently, his employer assumed that Singaporeans could benefit from the COVID-19 Recovery Grant, while the foreigners could not.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Unfortunately, this Singaporean applied for but was denied the COVID-19 Recovery Grant and, so, he ended up worse off than his foreign colleagues.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I will be making an appeal on his behalf directly to MSF but I hope MOF can consider ways to prevent companies from employing this form of arbitrage to reap the best of both worlds and, in the process, disadvantage Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In summary, Mr Deputy Speaker, I hope to see greater detail in the Government's roadmap for reopening.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The public needs a more easily understood COVID-19 Risk Index and we should make a strong push to overcome vaccine hesitancy in order to reduce the risks of serious COVID-19 infections.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Each nation has formulated its own strategy to lift restrictions and find ways to return to a more normal way of living, with UK leading the charge by declaring "Freedom Day".

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Developing COVID-19 resilience is crucial to securing and adapting Singapore's economic competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Yesterday, in Parliament, the MTF shared Singapore's roadmap towards treating the virus as endemic.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, some quarters remain sceptical how well this will be executed and carried through.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Just as we thought we had seen light at the end of the tunnel, the sudden roll-back to Phase Two (Heightened Alert) arising from the Jurong Fishery Port and KTV clusters dealt a fresh blow to businesses and the community at large.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst most understand the need to tighten restrictions until we achieve a higher vaccination rate, many Singaporeans wonder if the approach could have been better calibrated, such as allowing two fully-vaccinated diners to a table, instead of banning dining-in outright.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This consideration seems reasonable in light of the Government's earlier signal that Singapore should learn to live with an "endemic" COVID-19 in our midst; so that, with robust public health defences in place, we shift our focus from "Zero COVID-19" to "Living with COVID-19".

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We have developed enhanced testing and tracing capabilities, good control over infection rates, kept hospitalisation rates low and appeared to be able to ringfence the spread of infection.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We should expect "Living with COVID-19" to include intermittent outbreaks and even the emergence of new variants, every now and then.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Having worked so hard to build our defences, should we not be adopting a more confident posture?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As part of "Living with COVID-19", we should establish a suite of leading indicators that better predict the imposition of restrictions, so that businesses and the public are not constantly caught by surprise.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These indicators could be based on a combination of key health metrics, including infection rates, vaccination rates, hospitalisation rates, ICU admissions and fatalities – a so-called COVID-19 Index which businesses and individuals can monitor, for a shared sense of vigilance and ownership.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I guess, something similar to what Member Gerald Giam mentioned earlier.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We could guide Singaporeans to read and interpret this COVID-19 Index away from the focus on infection rates alone, which may shape their behaviour.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Affected businesses may also rely on a set of new norms to sustain their operations, from qualification for rental relief and contract variations to wage support and credit support, so that the burden is shared more fairly, every time restrictions are imposed.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They should not have to rely on the goodwill of landlords nor individual negotiation with financial institutions to keep the line of credit flowing each time restrictions are enforced.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There should also be a basic package of state-sponsored COVID-19 support that individuals and businesses can expect to kick in every time restrictions are announced, rather than uncertain drip-feed of measures that many believe are subject to negotiation and lobbying.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Minister for Trade and Industry yesterday urged businesses to get medically eligible staff to get vaccinated and to deploy unvaccinated employees to lower risk settings.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is in fact an existential issue for Singapore as an international business hub.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We survive and thrive on our ability to connect our businesses and people to the region and the world.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As other countries move more aggressively to reopen their borders, I am glad to hear that the prospect of travelling with few restrictions is in sight, if it comes through in early September.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I have heard senior regional executives beginning to question the value of being based in Singapore, as they are no longer able to travel freely in and out of the country for business.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Some are considering leaving for good, as it is no longer tenable for them to be separated from family and loved ones for such extended periods of time.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is bolstered by increasing adoption of "Work Anywhere" policies as well as new growth opportunities in their home countries.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singapore has managed to cushion itself from the unemployment hardship suffered by other countries because of COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Government spared no expense in supporting businesses to hire locals, with significant levels of Government funding directed towards the Jobs Support Scheme (JSS) and the Job Growth Incentive (JGI) scheme, including this round.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: While I applaud the success of the scheme, it is still unclear how businesses can make the transition without continued Government support.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The pandemic has evoked heightened awareness of such vulnerabilities and gaps.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Rather than keeping status quo, we should seize the moment to build consensus on how we may address these issues collectively.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The speed at which COVID-19 vaccines were developed served to remind us that, with the right conditions, major scientific breakthroughs, such as success of the “messenger RNA” technique behind the Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna vaccines, are possible.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We are also reminded that moving fast and removing barriers are the best things the Government can do.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, it is good that we kept this.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, this effort must be accompanied by the Government's intervention to ensure innovations are translated into real world solutions beyond the labs and scientific publications and are diffused through the economy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Businesses must be able to harness such technologies to raise productivity and, ultimately, contribute to higher living standards.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Research funding should be prioritised accordingly and be scrutinised to deliver economic value to the wider society.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These enterprises are the very examples of micro resilience that we need to cultivate as they are the seedlings of future enterprises, if properly nurtured.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To understand how we can support the acceleration process, we need to review if existing policies are conducive to current trends and to build support measures that lower barriers to entry, broaden the scope of economic activities and implement oversight frameworks for the industry to flourish.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But they should not be so onerous as to stifle these budding enterprises.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Let us transform our recovery to build back better, broader and stronger.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We did it before and we will do it again.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Community spread has increased and the large number of unlinked cases is cause for much concern, particularly when we have not yet reached our vaccination target of 70%.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While challenging, these restrictions are important to bring down our community infection levels and to ensure that our healthcare system and workers are not overwhelmed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I also note that we continue to make progress with our vaccination rollout and all the staff and personnel involved in this national effort to safeguard us against the virus have my utmost respect and gratitude.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The last two months, in particular, have been difficult ones for Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Both residents and businesses alike have had to navigate and respond to restrictions that have changed on an almost biweekly basis.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Other restrictions were also brought in to restrict social gatherings and, amongst others, the retail and fitness industries took a large hit.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Primary and Secondary schools also shifted to home-based learning.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even as diners, F&B businesses and other industries were celebrating a cautious return on 12 July, the now infamous KTV cluster was announced on that very day.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: One can only imagine the amount of losses that this has resulted in.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While I appreciate that our responses are, in some ways, shaped by the fast-changing nature of the pandemic, we should pause and reassess whether this approach of drip-feeding restrictions and business support measures is doing more harm than good.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Many business owners, in particular SME owners, have written to me to express their anguish over cashflow difficulties.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Retail, fitness, F&B and related businesses along the entire supply chain are on their knees from having endured more than 18 months of hardship arising from a reduction in footfall and various permutations of closures or restrictions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Many of them have said that they are clinging on and depend on a timely disbursement of a patchwork of business support schemes to stay afloat, even while they scramble each time to make sense of the ever-changing restrictions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Some SME owners have told us that while they can deal with tight restrictions and difficult regulations, what has been particularly difficult is the ever-changing landscape in which they are constantly spending a lot of time and energy adapting their businesses to comply with.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While we should encourage businesses to be nimble and adapt quickly to a rapidly changing environment, I fear that the last 18 months would be a step too far for all but a lucky few.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We cannot take the position that uncompetitive and inflexible businesses that are unable to pivot to deal with such times should be allowed to go under.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is also too much at stake, as many livelihoods depend on the survival of these businesses.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I believe the MTF is painfully aware of this.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, events over the last two weeks, in particular, have proven to be very confusing and disruptive.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The sudden changes just days apart have resulted in much stress and confusion and these also do not engender confidence, as many of us often wonder how many days or weeks will pass before a sudden change in position is on the cards again.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And even as we, as individuals, alongside our businesses, struggle to make sense of the shifting landscape, the vast majority of us here in Singapore do want to follow the rules and play our part in the fight against the disease.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is something to be applauded and should not be taken for granted.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is also up to the Government and us, as lawmakers, to ensure that there is a level of assurance, stability and, where possible, certainty in the measures we take and the support we give Singaporeans and our businesses.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While it may appear that calibrating business support schemes in accordance with the situation of the day allows for targeted support to be given, over prescribing or managing the situation may end up being self-defeating.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It could result in a situation where our policies become too reactive and the confusion and uncertainty that result may end up in help not reaching those who need it the most.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Attention also has to be paid to keep rules simple as much as possible, an approach in policy-making that we used to pride ourselves in.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, business owners struggle to make sense of the various schemes available to them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To top it off, they are also facing problems due to the delayed or uncertain nature relating to timing and amount of disbursements that they are eligible for.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If the intention is to support these businesses, we must make sure that our support is effective and is as efficient as possible.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These schemes must be designed to deal with the immediate threat faced by businesses which are already on the ropes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: COVID-19 will remain with us for a while yet and emerging variants may mean that our drive to handle this as endemic would suffer from setbacks.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The question is, therefore, how can we continue to provide our businesses with support in a sustainable manner?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We can keep on extending schemes at the very last minute and going through a budgeting process each time new restrictions are announced.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But what we need now, more than ever, is a roadmap with support measures pegged to respective restriction levels moving forward.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It would be extremely helpful to individuals and businesses to know what this roadmap is, with stages and criteria that are determined in advance and clearly communicated to all of us to enable us to plan forward as much as possible.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Next, I also note that, apart from businesses, individuals, too, are having to adapt to our changing times.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our economy has been kept afloat by new working arrangements becoming the norm, with working from home now being the default arrangement for many.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This has brought some unexpected conveniences for some, like allowing us more family time without the need to commute to the workplace.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, there are also some of us for whom working from home has not yielded good results.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This has been attributed to digital workloads rising due to the pandemic.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We need to bear their welfare in mind when we adjust our workplaces and jobs to reflect the new normal.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I also hope that the trends we see, with an increase in those pursuing non-traditional career paths, will continue and receive more attention.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Another group of workers which you must also consider is our essential workers, particularly those involved in the provision of the different types of care responsibilities and who work to keep our care infrastructure and essential infrastructure going.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The inability to work from home, shortage of manpower, coupled with the lack of travel opportunities for a break even if it is just a quick day trip across the border, means that our essential workers have been particularly hard hit.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Women, too, across all societies have borne the brunt of the pandemic and we are no exception in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Attention has to be paid to these groups to ensure that they are not pushed to the point of breaking, driven by the various workloads and household responsibilities with no chance for respite.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The pandemic has also highlighted the unsustainable nature of some of our industries and our economic model, which rely on cheap, abundant foreign labour.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Many construction projects have been delayed as a result.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps, this is the push we need to fully transform this sector and raise productivity levels to solve the labour crunch.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As I mentioned here in this House earlier in May, it is timely that our businesses take the first steps in transforming to move away from our addiction to cheap, abundant labour.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In his response earlier this month, the Health Minister said that it would not be realistic to provide a definitive roadmap.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And in a Facebook post on 20 July 2021, the Prime Minister said that Singapore has to "feel our way forward".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I would, therefore, like to seek clarification from the MTF about what is the definitive plan for how we move forward.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If so, will the Government, in the spirit of accountability and providing much needed stability and confidence, make these metrics and roadmaps public?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If there are obstacles to doing so, what are they and what can this House do legislatively to ease the process?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This would lead to less confusion and it behoves us to ensure that we have coherent policies that are communicated early and clearly, especially as we are a country that prides itself on doing well in rankings for the ease of doing business due to the clarity and transparency in our processes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Most of us accept that there are, indeed, times when restrictions need to be tightened at short notice as the situation develops rapidly.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, we need as much warning as possible to allow businesses and households a fighting chance to rework plans and try our best to stave off any impending cashflow crises.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is, therefore, important that we have clarity, such as the risk index proposed by my colleague Mr Gerald Giam, that is announced to the public.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Telling our people what the matrices which inform our decision-making are can only add to public confidence that the crisis is in good hands and let us know that our policymakers are dealing with it in a competent and coherent manner.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This approach is also important in addressing ground feedback relating to matters as wide-ranging as vaccine hesitancy to understanding the different restrictions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We owe much to our civil servants and various agencies who have been hard at work coming up with and implementing the various policies and schemes, but I also note that the details about communication matter, too, and they can make or break an individual’s reaction to our containment measures and fight against COVID-19.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, the changes and updates in vaccine safety and advice stemmed from an approach with an abundance of caution.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This often leads to the sense that the MTF is having to scramble to play catch-up each time major changes are announced.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There are three areas that I wish to touch on in my speech today: one, helping businesses cope with the disruptions of COVID-19; two, the COVID-19 Recovery Grant – Temporary scheme, to help lower- and middle-income individuals whose income has been impacted; and, three, mental wellness support for individuals and businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With more than a year and a half of living with COVID-19, while businesses are now more ready to adapt to the disruptions, demand and business volumes have taken a beating when operations have had to stop or scale back due to the various phases and, most recently, the Phase Two (Heightened Alert).

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For consumer-facing businesses, for example, food businesses, gyms, personal services, many have not been able to do dine-in or to continue offering their services during the Phase Two (Heightened Alert) and Phase Three A or have had to scale back significantly.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: However, overheads and ongoing business costs still need to be paid.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The support is important for businesses to stay afloat, adapt and pivot for the new normal as well as to enable workers to stay employed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The support measures announced for Phase Two (Heightened Alert), Phase Three (Heightened Alert) and this current Phase Two (Heightened Alert) are timely and much needed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Managing costs, however, can only go so far.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This prolonged disruption and the uncertainties have and will continue to impact cash flow for even the most prepared and sound businesses if demand and capacity to operate are significantly lower over a prolonged period of time.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To survive and to get back on track, businesses must be able to continue to do business.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The ways of disruptions have shown us that COVID-19 will be with us for some time and the new normal will include living with COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am thankful that the Ministers in their Ministerial Statements yesterday gave us a view of the roadmap of opening up.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This gives some idea of the steps and a line of sight of how businesses can expect in terms of going forward, albeit the caveat is still that we may continue to still face bumps or some bumps along the way.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We have to recognise that the cost of doing business has increased with the additional actions needed for the safe management measures.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Just to name a few, this includes additional manpower to ensure customer compliance with SMMs and regular testing of staff.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For the safety of everyone, SMMs are needed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, while giving relief to businesses to deal with the impact of COVID-19 has helped in the intermediate and the interim, we do need to find ways to better handle the cost of operating in the new normal as SMMs will still be required on an ongoing basis.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As businesses pivot and adapt with the new business models, there may be a need to also rethink the use of physical spaces.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For many businesses, rental cost is usually a major part of the operating costs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, as businesses transform, they may need less space or may need to relocate due to the changes in the type of space required.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Rental release and cost-sharing among stakeholders are welcomed in the short term but what help can there be to allow businesses the flexibility for amicable restructuring of tenancy contracts without significant penalties while cushioning some of the impact for landlords?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The expansion and the coverage of the scheme is intended to provide short-term support to lower- and middle-income employees and self-employed persons who suffer from sudden and significant income loss during this period.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Given that the pandemic has been ongoing for a year and a half and still is with us, the impact of COVID-19 on individuals has been prolonged and not just during this period of heightened alert.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Just like businesses, employees and self-employed persons have been dealing with the many waves over the last one and a half years since the outbreak.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As Minister Lawrence Wong had highlighted in the Ministerial Statement, "This has been a long and difficult journey." People have had to deal with the stress of adjusting and living with the restrictions and disruptions brought about by this pandemic.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This has affected everyone in the way we live, work and play.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The COVID-19 Mental Wellness Taskforce was formed late last year to review the impact of COVID-19, to take stock of the various initiatives introduced by the Government to support the mental needs of Singaporeans and to identify the gaps.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can the Minister share if more support will be given to help individuals cope with the stress and pressures brought about by the long-drawn pandemic?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What help can be given to employers to put in place the appropriate employee support programmes to promote mental health and wellness?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What more can be done to provide appropriate support for individuals?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To overcome the challenges that this pandemic brings requires all of us to do our part to keep Singapore and everyone safe.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Despite the current outbreak, we have made progress and I am confident that, together, we will emerge stronger.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: From the multiple permutations of what dine-in arrangements are allowed, which has spawned numerous memes and suggested PSLE questions, to a total ban on dining-in, F&B operators and consumers alike are frustrated by the capricious climate we have today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even as the Multi-Ministry Task Force shared an optimistic roadmap to reopening, we are still told that we must be prepared that the new variants can lead to more severe outbreaks and may well force us to introduce restrictions again from time to time.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, all businesses need a level of visibility in order to plan ahead, including adequate lead time to purchase fresh supplies and secure any additional staffing.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My colleague and Sengkang Member of Parliament Ms He Ting Ru has shared more about the importance of consistency in our restrictions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Because, to many businesses small or large, local or foreign, F&B or not, the Singapore which was known for business certainty and a stable, predictable regulatory framework is now seen to be supplanted by a capricious regulatory environment when it comes to the management of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Outside of the FAQs around the F&B and business sector and more generally, to many Singaporeans who have been tirelessly trying their best to cope with the pandemic over the last one and a half years, that light at the end of the tunnel now seems like the headlights of an incoming train.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Troubling as that metaphor may be, it is all the more important for us to think hard about how to better support our fellow Singaporeans at the present moment, while making fundamental changes to better prepare ourselves for the future.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My speech today will cover three main areas: supporting our workers, supporting our SMEs and supporting our future economy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I have earlier asked in a Parliamentary Question (PQ) on whether the Government can consider a limited trial of a four-day work week in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: COVID-19 has pushed companies to rapidly adopt new behaviours that would stick and change the trajectory of what it means to "work".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For instance, companies which are known to be averse to Flexible Work Arrangements (FWA) are now open to the idea of their employees working remotely.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A report by McKinsey has shown that 20% to 25% of the workforce in advanced economies could work from home between three and five days a week.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This represents four to five times more remote work than before the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While this study was conducted on a global level, it is evident that there has been a seismic shift in the workplace culture.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This brings me to my point of what it means to "work".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Over the past year, the idea of a shorter work week has resurfaced.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Prime Minister Lee had previously shared during the 2004 National Day Rally on the need for a better work-life balance.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I quote, "I am not sure why, but hours have become longer, the pace is more intense.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Maybe it's the Internet, maybe it's email, maybe it's globalisation, but whatever it is, you wake up at six o'clock in the morning, you check your email.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Eleven o'clock at night, before you go to sleep, you check it again and next morning, you come back, somebody replied at 2.00 am.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How to have children?" While not the only reason for our low birth rates, the five-day work week has gone beyond its intended definition and consumed our daily lives.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Echoing the Prime Minister's speech, the four-day work week is a pragmatic policy consideration that has been tried and tested by some companies and countries worldwide.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Iceland's four-day work week trials were also deemed "an overwhelming success", with trials in Spain also underway.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: That being said, I am conscious of the fact that not every employee has the privilege to complete their tasks in a four-day work week.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Those who deal with external parties, especially, are subject to the whims and fancies of their clients' schedule at times.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To institute a shorter work week, firstly, it is essential for us, as a society, to recognise the benefits in the form of not only the elusive productivity gain we have been searching for but, more importantly, focus on allowing people to become "fuller" people outside of their jobs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As what Microsoft had done, they have encouraged their employees to use the free time for "self-development and learning... for personal life and family care, social participation and community contribution".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we adopt a shorter work week with the right mindset, the benefits of better mental health, productivity and agency felt on the individual level will translate into society-wide benefits as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: First of all, I am comforted to hear from Minister Lawrence Wong that Singapore will preserve our sovereign tax rights and our rights to taxation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, while Minister Lawrence Wong shared in this response that our effective corporate tax rate is low, not just for MNCs, but for all companies, especially for SMEs in Singapore, I note from the data provided for the latest year of assessment (YA) 2019, that our effective corporate income tax rates are at a mere 3%, compared to statutory tax rates of 17%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Put in another way, for every $100 of profit, SMEs paid $11 to the Government in taxes versus non-SMEs who only paid $2.50 in corporate taxes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Could we not shift the incidence of taxation away from our local SMEs, which need all the support we can give, towards larger MNCs, which are better positioned financially and are currently paying a disproportionately lower share of corporate income taxes?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Rather than view global tax reforms as a threat, I see a clear opportunity for Singapore, given our global competitiveness and solid non-tax factors that make Singapore attractive to global MNCs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The key here is that global MNCs are not worse off if Singapore exercises our rights to taxation vis-a-vis the global minimum tax rates, but instead, given where effective tax rates in Singapore are today, Singaporeans will be able to benefit tremendously from the sizeable additional revenue headroom that could be generated from corporate income tax revenues should these reforms be enacted globally come 2023.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps by then, it would be timely for us to revisit the issue of raising GST from 7% to 9%!

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Another point on the support for SMEs relate to the Job Support Scheme, or JSS.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise that the extension of JSS support that MOF has provided will go some way in providing affected sectors some cost relief.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: After all, every dollar counts in this tight business environment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I also recognise that some sectors have been more affected by COVID-19, hence, the differentiated JSS support.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, as I have said in my speech in the debate on the Ministerial Statement in October last year, it would be more effective to direct a higher proportion of JSS payouts from the scheme towards SMEs, which make up a bigger proportion of jobs saved in comparison to large MNCs, which tend to have more resources on hand to tide them through the crisis.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A global fast food chain with more than $20 billion of revenues, for example, could certainly weather the crisis much better than our neighbourhood coffeeshop uncle selling wanton mee.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is a staggering eight times more than the 20,000 year-on-year decline in employment numbers for non-SMEs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If the role of JSS is to allow companies to better retain their local employees, then the results do leave much to be desired on this front.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This brings me to my third point about supporting our future economy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While the current relief measures are no doubt useful and could be funded via a reallocation of resources, ultimately, we may need to think of implementing automatic stabilisers instead of discretionary ad hoc schemes, as I have mentioned in my maiden speech.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In a policy brief published in January 2021 by the Peterson Institute for International Economics, Peter Orszag, Robert Rubin and Joseph Stiglitz called for the idea of a semi-autonomous discretionary fiscal architecture based on automatic stabilisers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: They proposed a new approach in which "fiscal discretion is retained but exercised after making the budget adjust more automatically and rapidly in areas where there is broad consensus that doing so is consistent with achieving broader societal goals." Using an example in the local context, direct assistance to companies, such as JSS, could arguably provide indirect support to employment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, many have still lost their jobs, even as the companies they work for receive JSS subsidies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Rather than providing blanket wage subsidies across companies, it is perhaps the workers themselves who are most in need of direct support and financial buffers in the event of unemployment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Workers’ Party has been calling for an unemployment insurance scheme for years and I am glad that others in this House, such as the hon Mr Patrick Tay, who also recognised earlier this year that it is timely for us to consider introducing some form of unemployment insurance.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I look forward to hearing more about progress in that area.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To conclude, Mr Deputy Speaker, I am heartened by Finance Minister Lawrence Wong’s assurance that the Government will not hesitate to use the full measure of our fiscal firepower to protect the lives and livelihoods of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I hope the Government will follow through on its assurance and give due consideration to the pointers I have brought up today, to support our workers, our companies and our future.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am in support of the additional support measures for Phase Two and Phase Three (Heightened Alert).

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I would like to raise two clarifications: one, on the additional assistance for some affected individuals and, two, clarification on the transition roadmap.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: JSS support has been well-received across some of the affected industries.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, the reality is that the pandemic has affected different groups of people to different extents.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of the groups that has been very badly affected are our freelance team sports coaches.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While there are other freelancers, such as gym instructors and tuition teachers that have pivoted effectively and gone online, the incomes of team sports coaches, such as for hockey, floorball, netball and football, have seen a drastic decline as they face an uphill struggle to move their trade online.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This concern was echoed by Mr Vijayan, Head Coach of Maruti Hockey Academy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Under normal circumstances, these coaches will be physically coaching for 30 to 34 hours per week but during the Heightened Alert period, they are only able to provide at most 10 hours of Zoom training sessions per week.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Similarly, the owner of Youth Floorball Academy, Mr Norani Zaini, and another Pasir Ris resident, Mr Rizal Rais who was previously the football coach at White Sands Primary, shared that their incomes had been generally reduced by more than 20% and, in the months of the Heightened Alert, it can be reduced by more than 50% to 60%.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Freelance team sports coaches are often paid an hourly rate.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The nature of team sports makes it difficult for effective coaching through Zoom.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Yet, despite these challenges, they have held on, persevered and, even in such adversity, continued to coach, hoping that the situation will get better soon.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At times, they even do it for free!

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Because of their passion to coach our young athletes and their desire to see the sports, such as netball, hockey, football and floorball, continue to grow despite this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is especially pertinent with the Tokyo Olympics going on even as we speak.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We should continue to support the growth and development of our coaches and sportsmen, especially at the grassroots level, where they already face considerable challenges even under normal circumstances.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can the Government consider extending more support for these affected individuals?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Another vulnerable group is our market and hawker stallholders.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, I am glad to hear about the support packages for them, including rental relief, the Market and Hawker Centre Relief Fund and Food Delivery Booster Package.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I would also like to inquire on the progress of the SG Together Alliance for Action (AfA) - Online Ordering for Hawkers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we quickly get more of them on board?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond these groups of workers, many others have had their income affected, too.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The situation is more strained this time as it is not just about entering into another round of Heightened Alert; it is the broader challenge of having to endure more than one and a half years of restrictions and continued disruptions to their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many have shared that they have exhausted their savings during this period.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am heartened to note that the Minister and fellow MTF Co-Chairs have been preparing a roadmap for Singapore to transit to a scenario where we learn to live normally with COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can the Minister share when we can expect the roadmap to be completed and shared in greater detail?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I look forward to hearing the details about the roadmap.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given that our target is 80% by September and we still have many seniors who are unvaccinated, do we have sufficient teams to do the mobile vaccination?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How are we increasing the capability and capacity of our healthcare system to better manage the possibility of more infections that may arise from the gradual reopening of our economy, even if they are possibly less severe?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What else can we do differently to reach out and encourage more people to be vaccinated to achieve our 80% target?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Have we deliberated on the risks of vaccinating children under 12 or should we extend the unvaccinated children under 12 to do home-based learning while we overcome this transition?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, we must take into consideration that there are people currently employed in temporary COVID-19-related roles, such as swabbers, safe entry screeners, Safe Distancing Ambassadors and vaccination staff.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These temporary roles may no longer be required as more and more people are vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What can we do now to avoid a situation of structural unemployment for these workers in temporary COVID-19-related roles as we prepare for the transition to normalcy?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   	While the JSS has been able to provide support for industries and individuals affected by the pandemic, the reality is that the pandemic has affected different groups of people to different extents.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of the groups of people who have been very badly affected by the pandemic are our freelance team sports coaches, such as those providing coaching services for hockey, netball, floorball and soccer.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It has not been easy for them to conduct the training online and, as such, they have seen a drastic drop in their income during Phase Two.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Despite these challenges, these coaches remain positive and strong.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As the Malay proverb goes, one must see through any task, regardless of how difficult it may be.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In fact, there are those who provide free training!

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Coaches like Mr Rizal Rais, a football coach, Mdm Sa'adiah Khamis, a netball head coach, and Mr Norani Zaini, owner of the Youth Floorball Academy, did it out of their interest to teach young athletes and their hopes of seeing the sport grow even during this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can the Government consider more assistance for these individuals?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I also support the help given to food stall owners and stalls in the markets.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition to these workers, many have also experienced declining incomes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The situation is getting tougher this time around as this is not just about losing income during Phase Two, but it is a broader challenge as they have experienced restrictions for over one and a half years and their livelihoods were disrupted during this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some have also stated that they have exhausted their savings during this period.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Minister has outlined in the Transition Roadmap where we can return to some degree of normalcy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To achieve this, more people have to be vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, we must find more ways to reach out not only to our seniors, but to every segment of our community to encourage them to get vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In Pasir Ris-Punggol, the M3 volunteers visited elderly residents who have not taken the vaccine to encourage them to be vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can our community encourage those who have not been vaccinated to take the vaccine to protect themselves and their families?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With more people vaccinated, we would be more confident in reopening the economy and allowing greater freedom to gather with family and friends, to travel for business and pleasure, as well as to participate in religious activities together.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Jobs, such as swabbers and Safe Distancing Ambassadors, will not be so critical as we transit into a more normal situation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must provide support for such workers to face this transition so that they will not be caught in a situation where they find themselves unemployed or unable to contribute meaningfully to the economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Let me conclude in English, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notwithstanding the above, I stand in support of the additional support measures for the Phase Two and Phase Three (Heightened Alert).

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.35 pm.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.20 pm until 4.35 pm.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: As of today, we have been battling COVID-19 for slightly over one and a half years.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Apart from the significant socio-economic challenges faced, COVID-19 has taken an unprecedented toll on our mental health and will continue to do so during our transition to a new normal.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: In my speech today, I want to focus on the mental health of our students and supporting our arts, entertainment and recreation sectors.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The term "COVID-19 fatigue" has become part of our everyday speech.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Almost everyone I speak to has experienced mental fatigue and tiredness in coping with the impact of COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: As adults, we feel this acutely, be it in trying to keep businesses afloat, looking after the safety of our families, adjusting to frequent changes in restrictions or the barrage of negative news.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: But we need to pay closer attention to our younger generation.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: This pandemic is happening, for them, in their formative years and will shape their perspective on life as they go on to become adults.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Students are a group who may be especially vulnerable to the long-lasting mental health toll.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I note that the Government also acknowledges the scarring effect that school closures have on learning and that some sense of normalcy is needed for our students.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: As our schools remain open, I am also glad to know that there are stringent safe management measures being adopted in our schools to prevent school-based COVID-19 transmission.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: But following these measures can take its toll on students too.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Co-curricular activities have sometimes been halted, celebration and orientation activities have been scaled back.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Such safe distancing has led to reduced interactions with peers that are so important for the development of social skills.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I am glad to know that CCAs will resume soon.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: While necessary, given the current situation, the schooling experience of our students today is vastly different from what it was pre-COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Coupled with a more uncertain future, these circumstances may lead to unhealthy pessimism and mental health issues taking root among our students, including recent graduates.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Looking back at my educational journey – and, for me, it was not too long ago – I am reminded of the extremely stressful points.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: We were lucky then in being able to release some of the pressures through social activities, such as going to the movies with friends and meeting extended family members.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: With the uncertainty of the pandemic, our children have not been able to do the same.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I worry about the effects that may result, given that they are already in a stressful educational environment.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: In recent years, there has been increased awareness surrounding youth mental health, with mental health education being incorporated into the Character and Citizenship Education curriculum from this year and groups formed to raise mental health awareness and stress among youths.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: These are definitely important steps in the right direction.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I hope we can have more conversations on mental health among students, a topic that the President recently raised following the tragic event at River Valley High School.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps, we need to re-evaluate how we approach mental health in our educational institutions, incorporating some activities to deal with the impacts of COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The Minister for Education has just shared with Members and the public the resources and capacities we have available to support our students and staff and the near-term policies MOE is implementing to address mental health issues.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: During the tough months of the circuit breaker last year and in the past one and a half years, people from all over the world have turned to various forms of entertainment to keep themselves healthy.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The arts and recreation sectors are crucial to our mental health wellness and it is integral we keep them alive and survive the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Those affected include performance groups, art theatres and even gyms, all of which provide Singaporeans with ways to unwind and de-stress and work on their physical health.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I appreciate the various grants the Government has introduced in Budgets 2020 and 2021 to support the arts and sports sectors.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Safe management measures have a sizeable impact on the bottom lines in these sectors, as not all of these activities can be easily moved online.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: These challenging times may lead people to pivot out of these sectors, as they look for ways to survive economically.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: For example, in February this year, a Mr Chiya Amos penned his experience in TodayOnline.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Mr Amos worked as a conductor in opera houses prior to the pandemic, but now works with Foodpanda making deliveries.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: His story is admirable, as it shows his strength and resilience, but it also compels me to think if there is more that we can do to support individuals like him.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Our arts and recreation sectors include many independent contractors and Singaporean-owned businesses.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Uncertainty caused by the pandemic, especially that surrounding their livelihoods, will inevitably add to the toll on such business owners and potentially create long-term scarring of these sectors.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Can the Government provide an update on how it is looking to partner and understand the concerns of the businesses serving the arts and recreation sectors and help them work through the issues they face?

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I recently spoke to a resident of Compassvale who started her own business partnership before the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Her father is the owner of a gym.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Both of them shared with me that before the pandemic, both businesses were doing well and that they were able to pay their workers fairly and make a profit.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: After the pandemic, however, they have been struggling.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: They have had to let staff go and are even considering closing their businesses.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I believe we can do more to support these enterprises.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Among these are socio-economic consequences as well as psychological ones.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: This is a time where we need to support one another.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Part of this is to make sure that assistance is going where it is needed most.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: More broadly, mental health issues can fester if ignored.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: If we are not careful, we may risk a generation of students who have to grapple with mental health issues over the longer term.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: In October last year, I spoke in this House calling for greater awareness on the importance of mental health.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Awareness on the issue has since improved, with more open discussions, but more can and should be done.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The mental health impact of COVID-19, which is a worldwide phenomenon, can have real implications for well-being in our society.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I ask policymakers and fellow Singaporeans to continue to treat this issue with the urgency and openness it deserves.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Hon Deputy Speaker, thank you for the opportunity to participate in this debate.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
