text: There has been a lot of angst felt by everyone across the board since the COVID-19 virus reared its ugly head some 18 months ago and continues to reach through communities across the globe causing healthcare crises, economic upheavals and putting individuals' mental well-being at risk.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Like many Singaporeans and businesses in Singapore, I am grateful that we are riding this storm with our Multi-Ministry Task Force (MTF) as captains.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: A big shout-out to the MTF and their crew for all they are doing to keep the rest of us safe and to ready our ship to sail the high waters, as we prepare to transition from pandemic to endemic and reopen our borders and our economy to the new normal.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Yesterday, in Parliament, our MTF Ministers had given us reason to be cautiously confident of what is to come.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: But it will take all of us, with a collective will, to see us through this crisis safely, to be there for each other and to be responsible for our actions, not simply for our own good, but for the common good of our society and the world.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Since the start of COVID-19, Government agencies have been working very closely with SBF, the trade associations and chambers (TACs) to understand the disruptions faced by the different industries and to help businesses navigate the uncertainties of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Government's support measures throughout the pandemic have been critical in supporting lives and livelihoods and these efforts are very much appreciated.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The recent return to Heightened Alert was a major blow to all of us.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It was unexpected and disappointing even if we do understand the necessity of the tough action taken by the MTF.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I have spoken to several of the TACs and they have all expressed appreciation for the quick action by MOF in reallocating funding to provide enhanced support to the sectors and the workers most affected by the Phase Two (Heightened Alert) measures.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Enhanced Job Support Scheme, rental reliefs, credit and other measures in the package will go a long way to help the affected businesses keep their staff and stay afloat.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: That said, many of the businesses are frustrated and worried about the future.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: TACs have shared with me that unlike last year, most businesses by now would have drawn down their reserves and savings considerably, and if their business does not pick up soon, some of them may not be able to sustain further losses.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Rental costs caused a pivoting to food delivery and their manpower woes are amongst what keep their members up at night.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Robinsons' closing down is the red flag for this sector.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For the nightlife sector which has been dealt a hard blow since the start of COVID-19, it is now bearing the brunt of the wrongdoings of a handful of errant operators who ran unlawful KTVs, the subject of which was much discussed yesterday in this Chamber.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore Nightlife Business Association (SNBA) had to put in a three-ring approach to recover from the KTV cluster and this includes the whistle-blowing system, industry pledge for transparency and compliance and call for severe penalty for the errant operators.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We need a sign of hope to move forward.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The business community is fully behind Prime Minister Lee's call to test, to trace, to vaccinate – I shall not sing for you – so that we can transition from pandemic to endemic as a community and a nation more safely and be ready to emerge stronger together.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is encouraging to hear Minister Ong Ye Kung's update in Parliament yesterday that Singapore's vaccination programme is progressing well, though there are still concerns with the vaccination rate and pace amongst the high-risk seniors.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We have to believe that, with all of the efforts of Team Singapore, we will get to the 80% coverage by the time we have the NDP Rally at the end of August.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Emerging Stronger Taskforce (EST) report that was rolled out in May-June 2021 has demonstrated that public-private partnerships with an action-oriented mindset can make things happen.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The EST and the various Alliances for Action, AfAs in short, have laid out a good roadmap for Singapore to get into gear to grow again post-pandemic.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Desmond Lee and Mr Tan Chong Meng, the co-chairs of the EST, had a webinar with SBF and TACs to share the process and the roadmap and to encourage businesses to engage with the various AfAs, as the companies plan their pivots and transformation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It was well-received and the feedback of the process had been positive.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The call to action is for our Singapore businesses, big and small, to join in the action.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The first one is access to foreign employees to overcome the labour shortage in all of our service sectors.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses hope that, as Singapore reopens, the following suggestions can be considered.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Government to review policies to ease inter-company and intra-company transfer of foreign manpower.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This morning, I think the Minister of State did talk about this during the Parliamentary Question session, but more details can be provided.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Government to review policies to ease inter-company ongoing efforts, such as the Place and Train Programme, that allow employees in affected sectors to temporarily move to another company or sector are positive interventions and it is hoped that it will be continued.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, I agree with some hon Members who have mentioned that we must keep an eye on or be on the lookout for, when this is over, how do we ensure that they are transitioned, trained to move into permanent jobs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Since I am speaking about foreign labour, I guess I do have to say a few words of what the businesses think in this space.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: While there has been a plethora of initiatives by both the Government and businesses to support digitalisation, increase productivity and redesign of jobs, it will not be possible to eliminate the need for foreign workers completely.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses have been encouraged, both by the industry themselves as well as by the Government, to use technology, train and upskill supposedly unattractive job roles, enhancing the value-add of the job roles and, in so doing, improving the salary compensation to make these jobs more attractive for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) Managing Director, Mr Ravi Menon, in his recent Institute of Policy (IPS) IPS-Nathan Lecture Series lecture on "The Four Horsemen", spoke about professionalising every job in Singapore, where every worker who undergoes continuous learning and certification throughout his or her career, is recognised for his or her craftsmanship, is valued by the consumers for their services, goes about his or her work with dignity and earns the higher pay that goes with the job.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In this scenario, hopefully, more Singaporeans will want to do these jobs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: But until then, we simply do not have enough Singaporeans to do the work that is needed at the worksites, in the data centres, in the kitchens and so forth.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There are also jobs in certain sectors where there are skills mismatch, or supply-demand mismatch, such as in advanced AI, deep tech, software engineering, in the IT sector and technology-related jobs across industries.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Minister for Manpower Dr Tan See Leng, in his response to the Adjournment Motion on Singaporean Core yesterday, shared that MOM has set up tripartite committees across the board to work on this issue.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that there will be a good outcome for all: the Singaporean workers, the companies and our Singapore, the little red dot.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Still, I will appeal to the good sense of my fellow Singaporeans to recognise that foreign talents complement our local Singaporean workforce and we need each other.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Several other Members of the House have also talked about this and I must say that there have been many Government COVID-19 relief measures rolled out to help our businesses and our workforce.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: But the best help, of course, is to bring back the business for the companies.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Most Singapore SMEs have very low digital maturity score.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In the new normal, however, digitalisation and connectivity are critical for survival and growth.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: IMDA has been making credible efforts to bring our SMEs along with SMEs Go Digital, Hawkers Go Digital and the multitude of initiatives and campaigns.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: A key reason for their acceleration to e-payment is the strong support by the IMDA's Digital Office.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The IMDA's Digital Office staff practically hold their hands to get across the line.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The same support will be needed if we are to help the hawkers and merchants adopt online ordering and delivery platforms.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And I submit to you, similar support is likely to be needed for SMEs across other industries.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With the Phase Two (Heightened Alert), sales activities are muted.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Though some projects sell well, there are many which are very slow moving and likely to hit Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD) penalty if no extension is granted.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For the hotel, entertainment and tourism industries, establishments have been badly affected by the pandemic due to the small domestic market and lack of tourists.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses all hope that Singapore, with our increased vaccination coverage, will further expand green lanes and trial "Passports for Vaccinated Visitors", to attract the return of tourists and business travellers to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As Minister Gan Kim Yong mentioned yesterday, we might want to trial with countries which have similarly high vaccination rates and also have a "health passport" system similar to Singapore's.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: My third point is reopening plan with ASEAN and our key trade partners, critical for Singapore's status as a regional HQ.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses are very appreciative of Singapore's approach to managing COVID-19 and ensuring our preparedness to enable Singapore to reopen its corridors in a controlled and safe manner.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: They would like to see the Government place importance on prioritising the opening of borders for business travel and home travel for both business and compassionate reasons.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There are many senior business leaders who are Employment Pass (EP) holders in Singapore by virtue of our hub status.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Since the start of COVID-19, many of them have not seen their families back home for more than a year.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our companies need to have the certainty that their staff who are EP holders returning home to see family, can return to Singapore to resume their work as per their employment agreement.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our companies are open to extensive testing and contact tracing and, where necessary, consider differentiated protocols to handle fully vaccinated individuals and those who are not vaccinated.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore Manufacturing Federation sees that it is an imperative for Singapore to collectively work towards the vision of ASEAN as the manufacturing hub if Singapore is to continue to stay relevant.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And public-private partnerships could be strengthened for internationalisation and regionalisation of local companies.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Especially in ASEAN, no one is safe until we are all safe.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Seeing Minister Vivian Balakrishnan's post on representing Singapore in delivering oxygen to Indonesia during their plight was absolutely the right thing to do.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our participation in donating vaccines to COVAX for poor countries is absolutely the right thing for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It will take time and we all need to be patient, but act now, we must.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that companies in Singapore rethink their corporate purpose and act together to lift and support the companies in their ecosystem by building greater capabilities, for example, digitalisation as strategic enabler and regionalisation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This is an imperative for Singapore and we need to enhance the hardware, software as well as the "heartware" of our businesses.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There is an urgent need to find ways to keep Singapore connected to the world and for businesses to find new business models that will enable Singapore to emerge stronger, post-pandemic.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It has been a long and painful journey in dealing with the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There is light, I believe, at the end of the tunnel but it will take our collective will and a strong sense of responsibility toward each other if we are to move smoothly towards the reopening of Singapore's economy and borders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is certainly more that can be done to offer short-term transitional support that the most vulnerable segments, especially displaced workers and those operating in the F&B and hospitality sectors, along with our local SMEs, as my Sengkang colleagues Mr Louis Chua and Ms He Ting Ru have pointed out.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I wish to focus instead on the longer-term elements of the Statement, especially surrounding SINGA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will pose three questions about spending reallocation, a timeline for bond issuance and the scheme for income-contingent student loans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My first question has to do with better understanding why the Government has decided to reallocate development expenditure from an underutilised Budget, instead of accelerating spending so that projects may be completed according to the original timeline.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, we should recognise that the delayed $0.6 billion in development expenditure has an opportunity cost in terms of foregone benefits from these capital projects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If we truly believe that the benefits of our development expenditures have not been irrevocably altered by pandemic-related delays – and I believe they should always be the case for long-term capital projects – then we should be working hard to get these delayed projects back on track by boosting immediate spending rather than passively accepting the delay.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will also allow the revenue streams associated with projects to accrue sooner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And, of course, this is not an abstract cost existing only on paper.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have many residents whose living situations have been significantly compromised by the delay in the expected handover dates of their BTO flats.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Could we not accelerate our spending, temporarily increase our inputs, so that the construction of these flats does not face an inordinate delay?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be entirely fair in our conversations with our contacts in the construction sector, they have shared that the ability to ramp up activity has been constrained not just by demand limitations, but also those of supply.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Construction raw material prices, like those of all commodities, have increased sharply worldwide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This spike has been further exacerbated by US infrastructure building, Chinese restrictions on material exports and difficulties in procuring Malaysian-manufactured materials due to its shutdown.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But activity has also been curtailed by some of our own policy decisions, which have served to dampen demand in the sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While we have attempted to relax some of the immigration controls, they remain comparatively restrictive and our friends in the industry share that this remains their most binding constraint.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Thus, while we recognise the importance of exercising caution to limit imported cases, as well as the longer-run need to transition away from low-cost labour in the construction sector, as my Aljunied colleague Mr Gerald Giam had shared, there is, in the meantime, an immediate need to relieve labour needs on this front.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, we know that well-executed quarantine procedures have proven their worth in containing spread along this channel.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Will the Government be willing to offer an update on their plans in restarting our inflow of foreign workers in this sector and the accompanying measures for managing imported cases?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, mandatory quarantine routine testing and safe distancing measures all have added to costs, which, inevitably, renders some projects no longer economically viable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Could some of these overheads be partially offset by the Government to help the sector as it tries to get back on its feet?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And, ultimately, the surfeit of projects could potentially have lasting consequences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our sources also report that skilled workers are leaving, hollowing out a sector already struggling with low productivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another important question, Mdm Deputy Speaker, is to enquire about whether the Government has a detailed plan for upcoming SINGA bond issuance, or if it plans to dip into markets on a more ad hoc basis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will contend that we require not just a clear, if amendable, issuance timetable, but also one that is front-loaded as much as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, it is useful to keep in mind that low interest rates will not remain with us indefinitely.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This rate remained elevated through most of the second quarter, before easing significantly to around 1.3% in more recent times.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Surveys of market forecasters suggest that the rise in rates through mid-2022 may only be slightly higher than 2%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On its face, then, it may seem like we have ample time to return to markets for our future infrastructure borrowing needs but markets are unlikely to remain quiescent forever.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, a more careful consideration of the underlying components of long-term yields reveals that since mid-May this year, the real long-term interest rate – that is, the true underlying cost of capital – began to rise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What this means, in practical terms, is that as markets normalise, surplus capital is beginning to be dissipated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Once this process takes hold, we should expect a more decisive climb in the observed long-term interest rate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As I had previously documented in my two prior Parliamentary interventions on the issue, one of the main advantages underlying SINGA is the ability to lock in current low financing costs for long-term projects that we fully expect to realise and that will disappear or, at the least, face a much higher hurdle rate to justify the debt incurred if we do not seize the day.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Put another way, once interest rates begin an inexorable climb, many projects will no longer be economically justifiable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I should also add, before I proceed further, that I am an educator at an Institute of Higher Learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To reiterate, the idea is to use SINGA to seed a fund for income-contingent loans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government commits to fund all the costs of tertiary or continuing education programmes upfront, perhaps subject to a very, very modest co-payment as collateral.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As the graduate secures a job and contingent on them earning enough, the recipient would then pay off the acquired debt.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Just as important, such loans stand apart from SkillsFuture, because it will cover the full cost of an extended training programme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It will also not be constrained by the need to identify employer matches as the Work-Study Degree programme is.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And it is meant to be accessible to young, college-age students rather than mainly targeted at reskilling displaced workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such schemes already exist elsewhere in the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the United Kingdom, the government runs student loans, companies operate several plans where incomes must cross a fixed weekly or monthly threshold before loan repayment deductions are made.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the United States, various permutations of the programme have been proposed and implemented since 1971, enjoying bipartisan support and has been championed most recently by the Institute for College Access and Success.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Australia, Hungary, New Zealand, the Netherlands and South Korea have all introduced various variations of the scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, such a programme in the local context will also free parents of tertiary students from the perceived need to finance their children's University education, especially when their parents' CPF funds are already stretched in terms of meeting retirement needs and, all the more, by the income shocks endured during the pandemic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Since human capital investments, as a whole, pay off in the long run, such an investment is eminently suitable for funding via the long-term bond issuance under the auspices of SINGA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And, most importantly, surely, nobody can credibly argue that education should not be considered infrastructure in our 21st century economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Notwithstanding these three questions, Mdm Deputy Speaker, I support the Statements.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The COVID-19 economic shock has the characteristics of a supply-induced contraction of gross national product.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The withdrawal of British forces from Singapore not long after our Independence similarly resulted in the supply-side contraction of our national output.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: One, there was the need to tackle the consequent decline in our gross national product and the loss of employment of large numbers of locally employed civilians, as well as enlisted personnel, due to layoffs, retrenchments.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Then, as now, I believe that there are three main thrusts in a comprehensive fiscal response that pays attention both to the short-term as well as to the long-term needs of our economy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: First, there is the need to provide immediate fiscal resources to keep businesses afloat and to save jobs.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In the 1968 Budget, it was announced that a number of measures had been undertaken to help redundant base workers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This included providing redundant workers liquidity during the period of their job search through the Central Provident Fund scheme, into which all gratuities were deposited and from which regular amounts could be drawn.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, the Government introduced a training scheme to equip them with skills for new occupations in industries.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Second, there is the need to identify new sources of growth even in the midst of this COVID-19 shock to steepen the trend growth path of the economy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In his speech, Dr Goh Keng Swee noted that the best guarantee that the adjustment to the economic shock brought about by the British withdrawal would be relatively prompt and painless was to ensure a sufficiently fast growth of the economy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Rapid economic growth, he argued, would lead to a rising demand for all categories of workers and, with this, there would be more job opportunities for retrenched workers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The support measures for Phase Two (Heightened Alert) being debated here under the Supplementary Bill should be seen in the context of Budget 2021 that was presented in Parliament in February this year.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: That Budget includes measures to structurally transform the economy to enable innovation to drive productivity growth.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Notably, the Jobs Growth Incentive (JGI), by subsidising the new hires of resident workers, acts to complement the JSS.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, even though there are immediate needs and we have to cater to the short-term challenges many Members have talked about for businesses, especially the ones that are domestically oriented, there is still a need in thinking about our policy that we keep our eye on how the trend growth would be like when the economy recovers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Third, even as we confront directly the challenges posed by COVID-19, there is still the need to recognise other fundamental spending needs of the country and to find the tax revenues to pay for the expected increased spending.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Dr Goh Keng Swee was upfront about the need to increase tax rates and introduce new taxes to meet the significant increase in defence expenditures, having said at the beginning of his speech that it was neither possible nor desirable to conceal increases of such magnitude.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: With the benefit of hindsight, we can see how we overcame that earlier challenge of British withdrawal as well as later challenges that arrived in each decade.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In the 1970s, the economy faced the challenge of stagflation, that is, stagnation combined with high inflation brought about by the oil crises; in the 1980s, around about 1984 and 1985, Singapore faced its sharpest recession; in the 1990s, Singapore faced the challenge of the Asian financial crisis; and in the "noughties", the economy faced the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, over this span of a few decades, despite the negative economic shocks, we were able to create new jobs.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It is true that when it sharply hit, the unemployment went up.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: But because we focused our policy on the trend growth, therefore creating new job vacancies, the unemployment rate then came down again.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: When we face a supply shock to our GDP, such as the decline of the GDP last year, when the economy rebounded, it rebounded with that experience we had in the past and we shaped the trend path of the economy, that would allow us to move and continue on a higher trend growth path.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: There is, therefore, reason to believe it is important that fiscal policy not only responds to short-term needs but it also sets the parameters to raise the economy’s trend growth path.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: And we have those few decades to look back to, to have encouragement from.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Looking back, it is inspiring to read how Dr Goh Keng Swee ended his 1968 Budget speech.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: He had no idea at that time how the future decades would look like.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This event is likely to be no less significant than our departure in 1965 from the Federation of Malaysia.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Since 1965, we have proved that as a separate economic entity, Singapore has a far greater survival potential than many people, here and elsewhere, had believed possible.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Phase Three (Heightened Alert) was in place by 14 June 2021, with two-person in-room dining.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Five-person in-room dining was later resumed on 12 July, only to be short-lived by a change back to two persons within one week from 19 July.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On 19 July itself, I was at a coffee shop in Hougang for my dinner after house visits.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It has been over a year since the circuit breaker was ended for the General Elections to take place, yet it has been an unsettling period of ups and downs for businesses as the country copes with successive, growing COVID-19 clusters.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Today, I would like to touch on three aspects: one, work from home; two, more systematic and consistent supervision of safe management measures in businesses and less abrupt, reactive changes for businesses; three, impact of dining restrictions on F&B outlets.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Government has continued to insist on work-from-home (WFH) as the default for many of our businesses and offices, with exceptions for small numbers to go back to office when necessary.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This may compel many to WFH as the default and going to office on only certain limited days of the week.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The argument goes that this will keep more people from taking public transport and congregate in larger numbers in their workplaces.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On the employees' end, many have, in fact, gotten used to WFH.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For those who are fortunately able to work effectively from their laptops or other devices away from the office, many even relish the flexibility of incorporating childcare and other domestic responsibilities, which is not a bad thing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have residents who are parents of toddlers, both fathers and mothers, who shared with me their concerns of less flexibility with childcare once they cease WFH and have to go back to the office full-time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On the other hand, the flexibility of working from home has its downsides.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, as emails come in at all times of the day, many find it difficult to draw the line between work and time off from work.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This takes a toll on rest, family time and even mental health.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There have also been more neighbours' disputes reported in the past year since the circuit breaker as more people stay at home.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On the employers' end, some businesses have adjusted to WFH and may not even go back to having an office with full daily staff attendance.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Again, for many others, WFH is not ideal for their business operations, whether for getting more businesses, for internal management, for employee supervision or for managing staff morale.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many businesses struggle with this uncertainty of how long this will last.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Beyond a short renewal to see if things get clearer in the following year, how do businesses plan their rental renewal, keeping their space pending a return to the pre-COVID-19 modus operandi or adopting, permanently, some degree of WFH like Mastercard or Prudential and perhaps downsize office spaces?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What is the roadmap that the Government has so far as far as WFH is concerned?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What exact targets do we have to hit?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Minister Gan Kim Yong, in answering the hon Member Sylvia Lim's question in Parliament not long ago, has shared some factors for the Government's consideration.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But as vaccination rates increase significantly next few months, can the Government consider setting clearer criteria or milestones so that businesses can also plan accordingly?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, a more systematic and consistent supervision of SMMs in businesses and less abrupt reactive changes for businesses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the early days of the circuit breaker, I remember that the criteria for law firms was not clear and some received indication that they could operate while others did not.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Indeed, businesses strive on certainty, and systematic and consistent supervision of safe management measures should be encouraged.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The recent KTV cluster highlighted what was not known to many Singaporeans previously, that some businesses in the nightlife industry had pivoted to F&B.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It was announced that all the staff will be tested and their SMM protocols will be inspected to ensure these are properly implemented and before they are allowed to resume F&B operations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Given the timing of the suspension, it looks like a direct reaction to the KTV cluster.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, I am concerned whether the abrupt two-week suspension is fair to all affected nightlife businesses which pivoted to F&B outlets, bearing in mind that many of the 400 over establishments may not have the same kind of business or operating conditions as KTV bars with social hostesses and, hence, should not be regarded as having the same risk level as the intimate KTV bars.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the first place, nightlife establishments were allowed to pivot to F&B outlets as a way for their businesses to survive and we heard this, too, in the House yesterday.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The rest had to dig into their pockets to do the conversion in the face of indefinite closure of their businesses in the earlier days.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: When they were allowed to operate as such, one would have expected that their premises were subjected to initial and subsequent regular inspections for compliance to safe management measures, for example, wearing of masks when not eating, safe distancing, kitchen and service hygiene and many others.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If such inspections were carried out on a regular basis, would not the SFA or other Government agencies have been reasonably assured of the SMM compliance of these outlets or, at the very least, those establishments which do not have the intimate KTV operations or have similar characteristics?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The abrupt closure of all premises would have been avoided.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Businesses need certainty and abrupt orders to cease business like this will cause sudden damaging losses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Moving ahead, I urge the Government to have a more proactive and consistent supervision of SMMs in businesses and avoid abrupt reactive changes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, impact of dining restrictions and other measures on the F&B industry.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What I have said above about businesses requiring certainties and avoiding abrupt, disruptive orders also apply to F&B outlets.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is, indeed, one sector that has constantly been affected by the changing COVID-19 phases: from the circuit breaker across the various Phase Two and Three sub-categories, from hawker centres, coffeeshops, food courts to cafes, restaurants and caterers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Drinks sales go down and soup-based food suffer more.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Mookata stores turn to online sales to mitigate their losses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Zi char stalls suffer as there are no group sit-downs to multi-dish dinners.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: WFH also meant that F&B businesses near workplaces and away from residential areas, for example, food centres like Amoy Street Food Centre or Lau Pau Sat suffer a drop in business.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So, when Phase Two (Heightened Alert) was reinstated recently, I remembered the many hawkers I spoke to in my constituency over the past year and made a mental note of how I think each would be faring the next few weeks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I cannot help feeling a sense of dread for many of them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Coffeeshop assistants or even local drinks promoters have been asked to do less work or even no work.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many caterers have suffered badly because of the lack of events over the past year and more so during the circuit breaker and Phase Two (Heightened Alert) periods.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I shudder to think of the outlook for them until more and larger-scale events with catering can take place.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many may not realise that stalls in canteens in schools and Institutes of Higher Learning are also affected.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In June, I met a resident during my house visit who runs a food stall in a Primary school canteen.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Her income went down during the Phase Two (Heightened Alert) in May, with more home-based learning (HBL).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Another resident shared with me how the family business of running a few food stalls in tertiary institutions was also quite seriously affected by the COVID-19-related closures and online classes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Have all such institutions waived or reduced rentals when students switched to HBL or online classes even before the Phase Two (Heightened Alert) in May?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Since the circuit breaker, life has not been easy for many in our F&B industry.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The year 2021 is proving to be another tough year for our businesses.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is also notable that smaller landlords who rely on rent as their main income will also be given fair consideration since they may not have the financial ability to sustain themselves.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some businesses have shared that since the last Phase Two (Heightened Alert) in May, they are still locked in discussions with their landlords on adequate rental support.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, I fully support the move by the Government to mandate the rental reliefs and believe that this will avoid inefficiencies derived from such protracted negotiations between landlords and tenants.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will also minimise disputes, misalignment of expectations and erosion of trust between landlords and tenants.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To confront COVID-19, the Government had introduced various support measures to help businesses cope with its impact.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Supply Bill has differentiated rent relief for companies solely based on revenue, which may not be sufficient to assess a company's ability to withstand long-drawn challenges like the one we are going through now.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My suggestion is that we consider adding the criteria of earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) for companies in industries that operate with low margins.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am aware that this would add additional administrative requirements but this would differentiate critical companies who need help from those who enjoy better margins because of the nature of their industries.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My second recommendation is for the Government to consider extending moratoriums for the Temporary Bridging Loans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Since 2020, businesses need help for moratoriums of loans, especially for sectors that are unable to restart core business activities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Through my engagements with some businesses, they shared with me that these Temporary Bridging Loans require them to make principal payments after a year while this pandemic has lasted way more than a year.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, with this current round of the Heightened Alert phase, businesses do require a much longer runway and even an additional principal payment moratorium.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is against the backdrop of suboptimal business activity for more than one and a half years.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I believe it is necessary for such an extension of principal moratoriums to provide businesses with this additional runway to restore cashflow, which dovetails with the overall COVID-19 resilience safe reopening plans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition to this recommendation, this is a good time to review the criteria to obtain a Temporary Bridging Loan, specifically, the need for preceding bank statements in applying for a Temporary Bridging Loan.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Unlike last year in 2020, when such a criterion could have shown how well the company was in 2019, its relevance now is clearly a problem because the preceding year was the ultra-difficult 2020.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A review of such criteria could well be needed to help our companies get through 2021.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My third suggestion is to further finetune the disbursement and criteria of JSS.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After close to one and a half years of battling COVID-19, many businesses are facing low cash reserves.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Through my conversations with several businesses, they hope for an earlier and quicker disbursement of JSS to aid their cashflow issues.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To quote one business owner, "We need water to arrive earlier to fight this fire." Some businesses have also shared with me how the Singapore Standard Industrial Classification (SSIC) categorisation of their businesses has a clear impact on the support measures they receive.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some businesses shared that due to their SSIC codes, they have fallen through the cracks.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This means they qualify for lower support measures, compared to those in the F&B, hotels and MICE industries when their work is highly integrated with them.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition, being classified as Tier 3 also meant that they will not receive loan moratorium extensions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The core events industry is intertwined with inbound corporate and leisure travel.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Each phase of dining-in restriction affects the confidence of event clients and leading to eventual cancellations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The continued cap on weddings guest size and suspension of social and community events have also meant lower revenue for event-related companies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This allows us to be more targeted in supporting our companies now and in the future.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must continue to hear the voices of Singaporeans from different industries and ensure that no one, no one, is left behind.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Targeted and equitable support that is commensurate with the impact specific businesses face is necessary.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These and earlier events have taken their toll financially as well as mentally on our communities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: At this point, I would like to express my deepest sympathies for the family and all those affected by the tragic incident at River Valley High School.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We cannot imagine the grief that they are facing and I would like for us to keep them in our thoughts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We need to take care of one another at this challenging time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: By SMEs, here I mean micro-businesses and small and medium-sized enterprises.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many who run or work in SMEs have been severely hurt economically after the last few rounds of restrictions, especially after coming out of a very challenging 2020.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many of those who run micro-businesses, in particular, work extremely hard.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Running a company or business can be very challenging, especially in the initial stages when most start-ups fail, but also when world-shaking events like COVID-19 happen.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Even in the best of times, entrepreneurs have to deal with curveballs on a regular, sometimes daily basis, as they grapple with issues related to winning and keeping difficult customers, retaining employees and ensuring cash flow.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As the founder of a company, I know this first hand.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The dot-com bubble burst around the time my company was founded, affecting many of our clients.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And about a year later, 9/11 happened, again, dealing a big blow to the economy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is often noted that this long COVID-19 pandemic has had a very uneven impact on individuals and on countries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Individuals who are better able to work from home have fared better, for example, as have countries with better access to vaccines.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What is less often noted is that COVID-19 has also worsened the inequality among companies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Those who are better able to adapt to the digital economy and to e-commerce have fared better.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Those in certain industries like biomedical, infocomm technology, food production and fast-moving consumer goods have fared, on the whole, very well during the pandemic, some seeing record profits.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Others in sectors dependent on tourism and travel, as well as retail and food services, have struggled with whole swathes of these industries being setback or wiped out.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should ensure that we create the right eco-system to enable these new start-ups and SMEs in general to flourish and both safeguard jobs in a competitive environment as well as contribute to job and GDP growth alongside MNCs and state-linked enterprises.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the rest of my speech, I shall outline some suggestions for nurturing our SMEs and, as I do so, I would also like to make a general observation first, as have many of my Parliamentary colleagues.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is crucial for our Government agencies to take the realities of running a business, especially an SME business, into account when formulating policies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Most SMEs do not have the manpower and capacity to digest and enforce complicated regulations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many SMEs operate on thin margins and a cash loss can have an outsized effect on their sustainability.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Another example is from the initially complex rules issued for dining-in earlier in July.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: How eateries were going to enforce those rules was something they grappled with.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some food service chains simply said it would limit dining-in to two persons to avoid the risks and costs of enforcement.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Let us strive towards fewer of such examples going forward.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Before I begin, I declare my interest as the CEO of a company, a research consultancy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It does not appear that such distributors qualify for JSS and I hope we can support them in some way.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some such firms I am aware of have already dutifully paid their suppliers for goods they have ordered in the expectation that dining-in would be allowed and are now paying an even higher cost to keep kegs and food produce in cold storage.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, one of my constituents also shared that his business did not qualify for JSS.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The line of business, listed as a secondary business activity, would by right, entitle him to JSS.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should also bear in mind that the revenue split between primary and secondary business can be fairly dynamic.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I hope we can take a balanced approach in administering this and other schemes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, we should also review the rental support given to SME tenants who rent a mixed-use property, that is, a shophouse for both retail and residential use.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Due to COVID-19, there are SME tenants who have to resort to renting a mixed-use property to keep their business afloat.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, doing so would seem to prevent them from obtaining the cash disbursements automatically.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some SME owners who are renting mixed-use properties find the process complicated to manage, sometimes due to language differences or unfamiliarity with Government applications.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, I would like to speak on the need to keep track of our SME schemes and this really speaks to more of our medium- and longer-term considerations about our SME ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Workers' Party Members of Parliament have filed many Parliamentary Questions over the years, keeping track of the outcomes of these schemes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But what would be more meaningful is to analyse the outcomes of these schemes, what marginal impact the schemes made to business success.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I know that this is not easy to measure; there is a problem of differentiating between correlation and causation, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But solutions to measurement problems can be found.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Publishing such outcome measures should be done from time to time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The case in point is the Productivity and Innovation Credit scheme which was discontinued earlier.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, we should improve the user experience for our grant applications for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In a previous speech in this House, I called for a one-stop portal for all citizens and companies to transact with the Government on assistance schemes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One such portal for SMEs now exists, businessgrants.gov.sg.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, it appears that not all the SME schemes across the whole all Government can be accessed on this portal.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I recall a number of letters, also to The Straits Times Forum page, explaining issues which users faced on this portal.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One such letter, dated 30 June this year, referred to an endless cycle of questions and answers because replies by email or phone call were not entertained.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Before leaving the subject, I should note that many SMEs still feel that the process for applying for grants and support is too administratively time-consuming and difficult.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Madam, I would like to speak on the need to nurture entrepreneurship and small businesses for the long run and this starts with the very lifeblood of SMEs – people.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Partly because of stubborn mindsets and partly because of competition from MNCs and the public sector, SMEs are often not sufficiently attracting, retaining, developing and investing in their talent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is a vicious cycle that reduces their ability to offer quality goods and services as well as survive into the future.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: SMEs without talent do not do well and not doing well means they are discouraged from investing in their talent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are Government scholarships that allow scholars to take on roles in SMEs rather than in GLCs or other major companies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, some IMDA scholarships allow for this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Is this something the Government is putting effort into developing and expanding?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Co-marketing these scholarships with boutique SMEs that are leaders in their own right could be a way to push students to explore the breadth and depth of our SME ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It could well be that SME scholarships are not as attractive to many young Singaporeans as other types of scholarships, such as PSC or GLC scholarships.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This may attract some PSC Scholars who realise they would rather develop their career in the private sector.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Also, as times have changed, more young people are realising that SMEs and start-ups can offer exciting employment opportunities and this is something that can be built on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There have been hit drama series produced in Korea, America and elsewhere about the fast-paced world of start-ups.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There may be fresh opportunities these days to market SME scholarships to youth, if we are bold and ingenious in designing this kind of marketing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, on the talent deficit that many SMEs face.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Again, I would like to talk about the role of shared service providers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many SMEs struggle to hire people to fill vacancies, especially in fields like finance, human resources, administration and accounting, as the pool of locals qualified for such work is limited and there is competition from MNCs, GLCs and big professional service firms for such talent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: SMEs can outsource this work, but outsourced service providers often charge high fees.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some SMEs form relationships with individual freelancers to do such work on a part-time or flexible basis, but not all SMEs have access to such freelancers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such a shared service industry would potentially be a strategic industry for our SME development and having such firms providing such services at low prices on an ongoing basis would perhaps be more helpful to SMEs than many of our existing schemes which prioritise the partial funding of one-off consulting work.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If we have a good pool of such shared service players, SMEs can outsource much of this back-office work to these companies at reasonable costs, thus enabling entrepreneurs to focus more on their core business and core competences.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Technology can be leveraged to provide low-cost services.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Madam, I will speak on what more can be done for business succession planning, including exits via entrepreneurs selling their business.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I asked a Parliamentary Question about what the Government was doing on this front in 2017.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Nowadays, it is common to hear that the children of family business owners do not want to take over the business.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And it is hard for family business owners to be able to find acquirers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many such business owners may not have the skills to identify acquirers and pitch their business to those acquirers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, many would be unable to avail themselves of the services of M&A advisory firms or investment banks, as these usually handle deals above a certain size threshold and the SME’s valuation may fall below that threshold.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: All of this means that many SME owners may be unable to ensure the continuity of their business nor be able to monetise the value that they have created.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Instead, they may end up simply winding up the business – and we have seen quite a few examples of this happening during this long COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The other group of people who would lose out from this would be the long-time employees of such firms which close down.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A basic form of matchmaking could be set up via an online portal which allows potential buyers and sellers of small firms to express their interest, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would also note in passing that, in some countries with a vibrant SME landscape, institutions other than the state play the role of providing general strategic advice to SME owners on matters that include business succession planning.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such institutions include regional banks in Germany, Switzerland and Japan and the giant chaebols in Korea, some of whom take an interest in the SME suppliers within their ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But in Singapore, such traditions are, by and large, absent which explains the context for the suggestions I am making.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, another point relates to SMEs starting up overseas.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some foreign countries’ embassies and High Commissions provide such facilities for SMEs from their home countries in key global cities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such facilities would enable SMEs to rent a desk or a small office for a limited time, as they explore an overseas market or start their presence.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While such facilities are available commercially in most global cities, having Singapore SMEs use the same facility and having that co-located with the office of Enterprise Singapore and other Singapore Government agencies in-country would facilitate networking with Government and collaborations among Singapore firms in that overseas market.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Subsidised rental rates could also be provided to ease market entry.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Access to such facilities should, of course, be limited to SMEs and not extended to large firms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Madam, I would like to talk about financing the growth of SMEs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Back in 2010, the Economic Strategies Committee (ESC) mooted the option of establishing an EXIM bank but the Government concluded that gaps in trade financing could be addressed by expanding the suite of trade and internationalisation finance schemes under what was then International Enterprise (IE) Singapore, without the setting up of an EXIM bank.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Since then, Enterprise Singapore has launched various internationalisation finance schemes where the Government co-shares risks with participating financial institutions to support our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, I am not sure if all our SMEs feel that it is easy to secure financing, especially for overseas expansion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It should be noted that even with the Government sharing a high proportion of the risk, commercial banks may prefer other options to deploy their capital than lending to SMEs, as that still may be seen to carry some risks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Surveys still show that many SMEs believe that there are gaps in our financing ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Larger SMEs with a turnover of between S$10 million and S$100 million wanted easier access to funding and grants; and collateral-free loans for business transformation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While existing financing schemes have certainly helped some of our SMEs, it would be worth considering if the creation of an EXIM bank for SMEs could help us to reach greater outcomes in SME growth and development.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is sad to think that some companies have this perception of their own Government agencies but I have come across this perception in conversations with SME owners.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: I cannot emphasise enough how important this commitment is to the local and international business and investment communities who are making their long-term investment decisions into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Some have started to refer to Singapore as a "zero COVID-19 society", implying that we do not have the psychological resilience to transit into living with the virus.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: It is thus important for Singapore to signal our commitment clearly, not just to Singaporeans but also to the rest of the world our commitment.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: And it will be a great story to tell the world we will transit into the new normal through the methodical and pragmatic Singapore way.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Moving on, I would like to express that I support the Supplementary Supply and Budget Adjustments Bill and support the fact that, in this time of hardship, we must support one another where we can.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, we are living in exceptional times and the Government has the unenviable task of making difficult decisions like the need for a circuit breaker or the Heightened Alert.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: In essence, it has appropriated private resources to support certain segments of the value chain.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that these measures are extraordinary and even necessary, and the Government has explained that these unprecedented steps are not to be taken as the norm.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is fair to assume that the path to recovery will be long and arduous.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: It is also fair to assume that there will continue to be shocks and disruptions that will require the Government to activate decisive steps for future lockdowns or other responses.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: A critical part of Singapore’s foundation for its economic success is being business-friendly and transparent and demonstrating a respect for legal contracts.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: For example, what are the considerations to activate such interventions and whether intervention is limited to certain sectors or would be applied more broadly, if need be?

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Besides the actual substance of the policies, the signalling from the policies is also important, especially for the business and investment communities that are making decisions on future long-term commitments.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding my clarifications, I support the Supplementary Supply Bill.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am in favour of all the measures in the support package.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I appeal to the Minister to provide additional support to our SMEs through Enterprise Singapore (ESG).

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many of our SMEs are facing difficulties due to the prolonged pandemic crisis.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is because many financial institutions remain conservative, relying on old business models and track records, despite significant changes in our business environment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the face of COVID-19, rapid technological developments, climate disruptions and changes in geopolitical dynamics, our SMEs need capital to transform their businesses and become more competitive.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A higher risk-share by ESG will make it easier for our SMEs, especially newer companies, to get the necessary loans.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For local companies providing products and services to Government agencies, Ministries and Statutory Boards, such as PUB, LTA and HDB, financial institutions may be able to provide them with bigger loans at lower interest rates if Government-related receivables can be used as collaterals.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is because of the trust financiers or banks have in our Government agencies as excellent paymasters.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The flexibility to use these future cash flows as collaterals will be a big help to these contractors and suppliers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: IMDA implemented the nationwide e-invoicing network in 2019 to help businesses improve efficiency, reduce cost, enjoy faster payment and stay green at the same time.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This network is an extension of the International Peppol eDelivery Network which enables businesses to transact with other linked companies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The nationwide e-invoicing network was launched in January 2019 and the nationwide e-invoicing network was renamed as InvoiceNow in September 2020.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Singapore Government is one of the largest buyers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Have entities like MOF’s VITAL started to require that its suppliers submit the invoices through InvoiceNow?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is the optimal period or timing to catalyse digitalisation, especially when the SME suppliers need faster cashflows.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The first is for full waivers of foreign worker levies and work permit related fees until the end of the year.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The waivers will lighten the burdens on retailers and F&B operations as they have problems finding Singaporeans to fill positions in the frontline and back-end.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many of these jobs are now being done by foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The second request is for subsidies to be also given to distributors and food producers who are also suffering due to the reduction in demand.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):    My work in a bank has exposed me to several small and medium-sized enterprises which are facing many challenges, such as protecting the jobs of their employees, worrying about liquidity and also adjusting their mindset to digitalisation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: SMEs employ more than 60% of the local workforce.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Their survival also affects workers and their families.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I believe that the Government will, as always, help SMEs, but in the past two or three months, some areas have really experienced "roller coaster"-like changes in regulations, proceeding then stopping, turning on and then off, and some had been unable to recover.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope that the Government will take this opportunity to revisit some policies and to help some sectors pull through this winter in a more targeted manner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This action was all the more stark because of planned relaxation of numerous Safe Management Measures (SMMs) barely three weeks ago.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: One thing was very clear from their statements, which is the intent to move carefully and safely to reopen Singapore's economy and relax social restrictions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: That intent remains unaltered despite this big bump on the road towards that destination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: First, we now recognise that so long as our population is not sufficiently vaccinated, we will find it hard to accept COVID-19 big flare-ups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Yet, this is precisely what has happened to us over the last three weeks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, it can happen and it has happened and we have to find ways to de-risk quickly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: To de-risk as quickly as possible, we have to increase our vaccination rate as quickly as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In Chinese, there is a saying 夜长梦多, in other words, "when the night is long, there are many dreams", many things can happen if the period gets longer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: So, we have to keep it as short as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In pressing on with vaccination, we must note three aspects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: First, that our most vulnerable group, namely our seniors, have the lowest vaccination rate relative to other age groups in our population.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Therefore, it is obvious, and I think we all agree, that we must do our best and our utmost to vaccinate them soonest to protect them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Second, that children below the age of 12 are not being vaccinated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Because that segment of our population is not receiving vaccination, we have to "compensate" for that fact by pushing up the vaccination rates of the other age segments so as to attain population herd immunity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Third, that as we take steps to reopen our borders, the people entering Singapore may not be vaccinated and may bring the virus into Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: If these inflow numbers are large, their vaccination status may impact on our effective "onshore population" vaccination rate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Therefore, we have to take that into account in safeguarding our herd immunity threshold.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This again argues for vaccinating as high a proportion of our local population as possible to ensure that we have sufficient ballast.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We have no choice but to push hard and with great urgency.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And because we have to compensate for our unvaccinated young in order to achieve total population herd immunity, I am, therefore, also strongly in favour of maximum effort by tripartite partners to drive workforce vaccination, the working-age population.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This Phase Two (Heightened Alert) experience over these last three weeks should convince everyone that vaccination is good both for workers' health as well as for companies' business continuity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Second, we must keep our eye on getting ready to seize the upturn.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: It is true that the ups and downs in our prolonged war against COVID-19 have led to a certain listlessness and fatigue in our businesses and our people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But we must not let that take hold.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Instead, we must do more to direct the attention and energies of businesses and the population to the gradually brightening global prospects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: There is real hope and opportunity to be seized, provided we are ready.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
