text: And to be ready means that our industries and companies have to be innovative and competitive; and our workforce equipped with the skills, technologies and work arrangements to be effective in a post-COVID-19 or COVID-19-endemic world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This result can only be achieved through solid tripartite partnership at industry and firm levels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In particular, we must focus on three areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The requirements are constantly changing and changing quickly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: COVID-19 has forced companies to work much more flexibly and unconventionally in terms of how they arrange the manpower to get the work done.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Many companies learnt that they can better tap and keep talent and good workers, both female and male, when they are willing and able to adapt their manpower models.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is a lesson learnt, it has delivered results in selected occupation types within companies in all industries and we must not let that go to waste.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Learn the lesson and keep it for gain.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: A company's chances of success go up when it has a capable, engaged, cohesive workforce with high morale.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Achieving this in the context of an increasingly diverse Singapore workforce, diverse in race, nationality, age, comprising both genders with equal ability to contribute at work and so on, means that the different segments must feel that they are treated fairly and have a joint stake in the company's success.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In the context of mature workers, a topic very close to my heart, I say this: whether the companies give their mature workers fair consideration and opportunity to train and upgrade their skills to stay employable will be key to whether their mature workers feel fairly treated relative to younger cohorts and whether they feel happy to stay and contribute, or otherwise feel discriminated, disengaged and dispirited.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: On this, I was greatly encouraged when I heard the speech by Prof Hoon Hian Teck just now, when he recounted, even as we look back, how we do not just look at the "now" even though we have to solve the problems of the "now", but, at the same time, we must look at structural adjustments – how do we strengthen our core, our ability, our capabilities to create and fight for that better future – quoting then Deputy Prime Minister Goh Keng Swee.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I thought that is exactly right and that we are on the same page.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: COVID-19 has been a trying period for us all and we are now faced with the challenging task of understanding how our world and our society have been changed.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Many have felt the tangible repercussions of this period, be it via the loss of income or the many changes that we have had to make to keep ourselves and our loved ones safe.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: But COVID-19 has also brought about many intangible changes.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Many of us must deal with new and challenging circumstances that cause "pandemic fatigue" and mental health is on the decline for many.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: However, as mentioned by Minister Lawrence Wong, "For Singapore, we can take heart that we are in a much better position to deal with the pandemic now than at the start." I applaud the targeted support measures to help our businesses and individuals most impacted by the tightened restrictions.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: At NTUC, we have been working closely with all stakeholders to help both businesses and workers alike and we will continue to do so for as long as necessary.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This is no small feat and is, no doubt, aided by our policies, such as the Progressive Wage Model (PWM), to uplift these workers and the efforts of our tripartite partners.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Last month, the Tripartite Cluster for Cleaners announced their review of the Cleaning PWM and, earlier this month, the Tripartite Cluster for Lift and Escalator also released their recommendations for our lift and escalator maintenance workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: These reviews take reference from the objective of the Tripartite Workgroup on Lower-Wage Workers (TWG-LWW) to ensure that the wage growth in the PWM sectors can continue to outpace median wage growth.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I am aware of concerns on the ground regarding a potential increase in manpower costs and how this could impact customers and firms alike.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As I had mentioned in my previous speech, everyone has a part to play in creating a more caring and inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This, admittedly, may mean paying more but we are mindful of and share our partners' concerns to ensure that manpower costs remain sustainable for all to create better jobs with good working environment and increases in productivity.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By lowering the age eligibility, many more workers who may need help with their young families or the added financial help to upskill will be able to do so.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Increasing the WIS payout to our essential workers will also acknowledge the valuable role they play in our society and the social value of their jobs.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Beyond efforts like the PWMs and WIS, I am also encouraged by other efforts to support our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The Alliance for Action (AfA) for Lower-Wage Workers, for example, brought together people from different walks of life – students, business owners and unionists – with the aim to mobilise the community to support our workers through ground-up initiatives and help uplift their well-being.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: There are many promising ideas and I hope work will continue to develop these projects to show appreciation for our essential service workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: One of these ideas mentioned during the recent AfA engagement is the Rest Area Guidebook, which includes 2D and 3D designs of plug-and-play rest area configurations.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This complements the call made by the Labour Movement and our partners to provide our essential service workers with a more dignified and comfortable working environment, such as access to proper and reasonable rest areas.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I am also heartened by the news that the project team has connected with *SCAPE and the National Youth Council to set up a rest area for their outsourced workers, with youth volunteers taking up the role of befrienders to these workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I hope that in the months to come, we will be able to hear more of and about these ground-up initiatives.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):   	In conclusion, as we take steps as a nation towards a new way of living, there is a pressing need for all of us to step up and support the particularly vulnerable during these trying times.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As a society, we should do more to appreciate our lower-wage essential service workers and our migrant workers who have continued to work tirelessly during this pandemic to ensure that Singapore does not come to a standstill.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We owe them more than simply a word of thanks and we should work towards tangible ways to improve their wages, welfare and work prospects.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: (In English): In conclusion, I would like to thank the Government for the targeted support measures that have been put in place to help the businesses and individuals most impacted by the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: These have helped and will continue to help Singaporeans as we navigate this new normal.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC, as always, will continue to work hard to support all workers but I would also like to take this opportunity to call upon all of us – the Government, organisations and individuals alike – to offer our support when we can to those who have been particularly affected during these times.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Just when we thought we can grapple with it, we are faced with another major setback.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The daily local cases shot up, similar to when our migrant workers were impacted last year.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This time, it is much worse as the clusters are within our local population.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Honestly, I believe, as fellow Singaporeans, we only have ourselves to blame, especially for the KTV cluster.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This latest development must remind each and every one of us that we have the responsibility and we have to work together to overcome this crisis.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I was just a typical Singaporean who got on with his job daily and earned his keep.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: However, this opportunity has opened my eyes to the importance of the Budget announcements for our workers and fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I recalled there was a part in the Ministerial Statement that really heartened me as a union leader.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister emphasised the importance of raising the capabilities of our local workforce.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In my maiden speech earlier this year, I had called on employers to make our locals their employees of choice.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This call by the Minister strengthens the belief and importance of having our locals with the right capabilities and competencies in our workforce.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Industries, such as aerospace, tourism and food services, are severely impacted.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Some need to transit from one industry to another to ensure that they have some income to tide over this crisis.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The Labour Movement has strongly encouraged workers to take advantage of this downtime and go for training in several ways.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: There has been an increase in training allowance to support self-employed persons.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Unions have been pushing for employers to send workers for training before resorting to cost-cutting measures.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Union members can also embark on their own training by utilising their Union Training Assistance Programme (UTAP) benefit.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Government assistance schemes, such as the Career Support Programme, Professional Conversion Programme and Capability Transfer Programme, have helped to train and transform our local workforce.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, SG United programmes give employers the financial support to employ our fresh graduates and mid-career workers in times of such uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Without this, Singaporeans would find it challenging to find employment as businesses freeze or reduce their headcount.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Many of you have heard about NTUC's Company Training Committees (CTCs).

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This reflects the commitment and collaboration from both union leaders and management to not just train for the sake of training but to transform their workforce to be more productive and competitive for the new business models.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The union leaders have been focusing on three areas for training towards three outcomes: the training would be targeted at being adaptable, embracing new technology and, at the same time, deepening their technical capabilities.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This would make our workers better skilled, more productive and the unions will work closely with management to ensure our workers get better wages, better welfare and better work prospects.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We have heard enough of FTAs and CECA as a policy.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Now, let us hear what some of the workers have experienced on the ground.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: One union leader shared from his personal observation and experience on the disparity in employment contracts between locals and foreigners.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: He had a disappointing experience of seeing the contracts of his local colleagues not being renewed but foreigners on contracts being offered permanent roles.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Another union leader shared the pain in seeing groups of foreign talents that were hired with capabilities equivalent to our locals.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: He observed that the HR manager came from the same country as well.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: These are just two examples, but, in reality, there may be many such cases.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: There has been such feedback raised and we need more affected parties to come forward to report such incidents or observations.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I welcome this as a step in the right direction and I look forward to the recommendations from the Tripartite Committee.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that Singaporeans still welcome foreign talents if they help elevate our workforce capabilities, complement the development of local talents and contribute to our Singapore economy.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: However, the reliance on foreign talents should be mitigated with the available Government schemes to help upskill and transform our local workforce to seize these good-paying job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to take this opportunity to urge my fellow Singaporeans to continue believing in ourselves despite such competition.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Go out, acquire new skillsets, compete with the best to seize the jobs you want.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Do not lose heart over rejections and failures.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The Labour Movement is here with you, you will never walk alone.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: (In Malay):   	The COVID-19 crisis has changed the lives and livelihoods of many workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Some of them experienced pay cuts or even lost their jobs.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In MOF’s announcement on 5 July, what caught my eye was the part where the Finance Minister emphasised the importance of raising the capabilities of our local workforce.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This call by the Minister strengthens the belief and importance of having locals with the right capabilities and competencies in our workforce.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The Labour Movement has always encouraged workers to enhance their skillsets with new skills so that the workers can continue to compete for job opportunities with better outcomes.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This reflects the commitment and collaboration from both union leaders and management to not just train for the sake of training, but to also transform their workforce to be more productive and competitive for new business models.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The union leaders have been focusing on three areas of training to achieve three outcomes: the training would be targeted at being adaptable, embracing new technology and, at the same time, deepening technical capabilities.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This would make our workers better skilled and more productive.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We are all aware of sentiments regarding the workforce in the finance and banking sector involving the foreign workforce.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This issue will continue to stay with us and will not rest anytime soon.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: However, I believe that Singaporeans will welcome foreign talents, if they help elevate our workforce capabilities, complement the development of local talents and contribute to our Singapore economy.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: However, the reliance on foreign talents should be mitigated with the available Government schemes to help upskill and transform the local workforce.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to the recommendations from the Tripartite Committee in due course.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Madam, on behalf of my fellow union leaders, I would like to convey our deepest appreciation to all our fellow Singaporeans serving in the healthcare sector for their sacrifices in taking care of the COVID-19 patients.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Please press on, all of us will stand shoulder to shoulder in our fight against the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The proposed extensions to the Job Support Scheme, the Temporary Bridging Loan Programme and the Enhanced Enterprise Financing Scheme–Trade Loan (EFS-TL) will be vital in providing businesses with much-needed liquidity to stay afloat.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These will, in turn, help to save jobs in the most affected sectors and we, in the Labour Movement, are in full support of these measures.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In his speech, the Finance Minister also spoke about the realities of living with an endemic COVID-19 and how the Government is preparing a roadmap for Singapore to learn to live normally with the virus.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: My speech today will focus on the indirect impact that COVID-19 has had on two vulnerable segments of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They are our migrant workers and our PMEs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: More recently, three workers died within a period of five days in separate incidents in June.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to MOM, the workplace fatalities involved safety lapses, which mean that the accidents could have and should have been prevented.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The increase in workplace fatalities comes as we reopen our economy, with various tough safe management measures imposed at our worksites to curb the spread of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Examples include cohorting of workers, establishing split teams and making sure workers do not cross zones within the worksite and even within the dormitory.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While these measures have worked well in curbing the spread of the virus among our migrant workforce, have they inadvertently caused the rise in workplace accidents?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Some workers that I have spoken to tell me that they used to be able to spontaneously assist each other in high-risk tasks at the worksite, such as during heavy-lifting works.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But they cannot do so now, which means there are fewer eyes and hands to do the same dangerous work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Or perhaps the issue is fatigue caused by an acute shortage of manpower in the high-risk sectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Industry associations tell me that the reasons for their departure vary.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Some because they were homesick; others because they were terribly worried about their family members back home.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Companies have found it difficult to find replacement workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: So, more responsibilities are loaded onto their existing workforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This, inevitably, leads to worker fatigue, which research has linked to a higher risk of workplace fatalities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am glad that the Government has recently allowed a relaxation of requirements for construction companies to bring in additional manpower from less traditional sources.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Industry associations, too, have started a pilot to bring in migrant workers from India in a calibrated manner.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Is the number even close to the monthly outflow?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If we do not act now, we stand to lose more lives to workplace accidents than to COVID-19 since the outbreak began.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is a grim milestone that we hope not to see.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that the Government can review whether there is a causal link between the safe management measures imposed at high-risk worksites and the rise in workplace accidents and workplace fatalities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If so, can we adapt and review the cohorting and zoning rules if 100% of workers within the site are fully vaccinated?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Labour Movement reiterates our continued calls for all companies in Singapore to conduct refresher Workplace Safety and Health courses for their workers, especially for those who have been away from the worksite for an extended period.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I also urge companies to put in place strict measures to prevent untrained, uncertified workers from operating machineries and performing other high-risk tasks.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In fact, all companies should participate in the Safety Time Out called for by the Workplace Safety and Health Council so that they can review their safety practices at their worksites.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For the past 15 months, many of them have not been able to go out freely during their days off.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This has had an impact on their mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How does MOM intend to assist our migrant workers in overcoming the sense of social isolation that many in the dormitories are currently facing?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many have been working from home in the past 15 months and a growing number are facing mental health issues.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Labour Movement, too, has conducted our own ground sensing and about two-thirds of those we spoke to said they experienced difficulties distinguishing work and non-work hours when working from home.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This might be why Microsoft's Work Trend Index reported that 58% of workers in Singapore said they felt overworked, while 49% felt exhausted.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But despite our high stress levels, there remain significant barriers to seeking assistance.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Zaobao also recently reported a local study that found that individuals who suffer from mental health issues are more than two times likely to lose their jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope we can review and consider legislating some of the recommendations listed in the Tripartite Advisory on Mental Well-being at Workplaces.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If workplace burnout continues to be a key workplace mental health challenge, then we may very well need our very own Right to Disconnect legislation to safeguard our workers' mental resilience.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Labour Movement is taking the lead to make mental health support more accessible for our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We want EAP services to be available in all companies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many PMEs have also given me feedback that the prolonged work-from-home (WFH) arrangements have caused other tensions to emerge.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Neighbours now quarrel because of the slightest noise and smell.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Our homes are meant to be a safe space where we can live, work and play in peace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But I can empathise with both sides: the new homeowner trying to move into their new home as soon as possible and their neighbours trying to do an important work presentation virtually from home.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As telecommuting work arrangements become more prevalent, we must do more to ease the tensions between neighbours.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While the COVID-19 pandemic has caused global travel to come to a virtual standstill, the working landscape has become more globalised than ever.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The year-long WFH arrangement has normalised remote working and both employers and employees have started to realise that a mobile computing device with an Internet connection is all that is required to work globally.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I recently visited a large multinational company, where I met a Singaporean project manager who told me that he now manages multiple construction projects and tracks each worksite’s progress from the comfort of his living room.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Is our workforce prepared for this new reality?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What is being done to help Singaporeans tap on such global opportunities?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But, Madam, the reverse can also be true.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What is to stop local contractors from hiring foreign project managers who need not necessarily be based physically here?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What about the traditional IT, HR and finance jobs that can now be performed remotely from anywhere in the world?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These are questions better tackled sooner, rather than later.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With that, I support the measures put forth by the Finance Minister.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Good evening, Mdm Deputy Speaker, and thank you for allowing me to join this debate.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is not a large country, but we are a strong one.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We are known for decisiveness, solidarity amongst our people and business excellence.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We crawled, staggered and eventually walked through it with fewer casualties than many nations last year.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Phase Two (Heightened Alert) for these businesses is an existential threat.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The industry is grateful for the assistance given last year.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Some businesses have recovered while others have not.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: For those remaining, it is crucial to their survival to receive additional resources.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Many may not think of sports and fitness as a priority segment, but it is a part of the magic that brings Singaporeans together.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Because of Phase Two (Heightened Alert), sports are disrupted.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Teams cannot train because the maximum group size allowed to gather is two people; athletes cannot compete.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This creates an extra burden for our national sports associations and sportspersons.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Yesterday, the respective Ministers spoke about a roadmap for Singapore, which changes the posture from dealing with COVID-19 to living with COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I hope this roadmap marks the next chapter for a seemingly endless journey that is COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Many may know that I am an Olympian.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Many understand that it takes a lot of work to reach that level of competition.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: But many may not realise that the journey to the event matters more than the event itself.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This is because sports are a test of character.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They are a test of strength and, when one can make it to the pinnacle of achievement, sports become a vehicle of motivation and encouragement; a source of pride.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As we tune into the next 12 days of the Tokyo Olympic Games, we hope to witness many more amazing stories.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Ahmed Hafnaoui, the 18-year-old Tunisian who won the Gold in the men’s 400-metre freestyle, and Anna Kiesenofer, the Maths lecturer who rode solo the last 40 kilometres of the women’s cycling road race to win Gold and Singapore’s very own Chantal Liew whose qualification to the Olympic Games is historic in and of itself as our first marathon swimmer to participate in the Games.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: What is important is the journey and not the actual event.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Even on a non-competitive level, fitness benefits include a physically healthier population and stronger mental health for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: COVID-19 affects our entire society and the sports and fitness industry is no exception.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Additional resources in the relief Budget go a long way to ensure the industry’s survival.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Without extra funding, these businesses cannot operate despite their contribution to society.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It was allaying to hear from Minister Lawrence Wong's Ministerial Statement yesterday that additional support will be given to eligible businesses affected by Phase Two (Heightened Alert) protocols.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Landlords chasing tenants for rental arrears based on full rent have been causing a lot of hardship and pressure on businesses.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Even if tenants wish to cease their businesses, landlords have gone after, or threatened to go after the tenants for rental arrears and damages for landlords’ losses of rent until the end of their leases.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It would be good if MinLaw can legislate relief.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Such a break would enable tenants of privately-owned commercial properties to terminate their leases earlier without penalty if they show that their revenues have been significantly impacted.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, the Minister for Law can reconsider reintroducing the Re-Align Framework for a period for the sports and fitness industry as the industry has been badly affected this time around.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It would also be good if the disbursement of the relief packages could be expedited.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The previous support package from the last Phase Two (Heightened Alert) has not been disbursed.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: With the industry facing yet another set of heightened measures, it puts a strain on businesses.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Companies have gone for almost four months without much income, costs are the only constant that companies have to continue bearing.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As the hon Member Edward Chia shared earlier, businesses are facing low cash reserves.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We need water to come quickly to fight the fire.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The second group is freelancers and self-employed persons.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: As the hon Member Sharael Taha highlighted, the Phase Two (Heightened Alert) measures have hit coaches and trainers badly.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Safe management measures make it impossible to conduct sessions for teams; and pivoting to online instruction for some of these sports and fitness companies is impractical.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Can more support be given to our self-employed persons and freelancers?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, the National Sports Associations (NSAs) and the wider sporting ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: NSAs are the cornerstone of the sporting ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They develop their respective sports from developing the high performance pathways, development programmes and coaching and officiating capabilities.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: A significant amount of funding comes from sponsorship and participation fees through events.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: COVID-19 will, no doubt, leave a lasting impact on the sports and fitness industry, in the way businesses plan and operate; and in the way Singapore and its residents view and participate in sports and fitness activities.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: One thing we cannot allow is for COVID-19 to affect our pipeline and our sports ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: With your help, the Government can be a teammate the industry needs, to make it through the next checkpoint.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Hopefully, the last round, the last lap, the last hurdle.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I understand a reversal to Phase Two (Heightened Alert) is necessary, yet I hope this gives you more insight into the sports and fitness industry's needs and why it needs additional support.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We want to continue finding ways to keep citizens healthy despite a tightening of safety measures.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This may mean investment in technology to host more virtual sessions.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It may mean our coaches, teachers, trainers having to work longer hours to adapt to the safety measures.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It definitely means we want to ensure that we can survive and impact Singaporeans in a healthy and meaningful way.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We also want to ensure employees in this sector have a chance to keep and evolve in their jobs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, I hope the Government can also recognise that the problems sparked by this crisis are not just about money.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And on that note, I am glad that our Second Minister for Finance, Minister Indranee Rajah is now also the Minister in charge of the National Population and Talent Division.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today, I will offer three suggestions related to time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first suggestion is about childcare sick leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today, students are still being sent home from schools and childcare centres because they exhibit COVID-19 symptoms.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This practice started in 2020 and it continues today, more than 15 months later.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is a good policy and I support it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Schools and childcare centres are places with high levels of personal interaction.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Keeping symptomatic students at home protects other students and, in turn, protects their families.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But it is also a policy that creates huge challenges for parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even before the pandemic, parents had told me that it was not enough.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It was just enough to cover them for the six days when childcare centres close every year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Now, they have to take leave even when their young child has only a mild cough or sore throat.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What about those whose jobs do not allow them to WFH?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What about our frontline workers and essential workers who put their lives at risk for all of us?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have spoken to teachers at childcare centres.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They describe how some parents plead and beg them to simply keep the child at the sick bay.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The parents say, "I cannot take another day off work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I really cannot." The answer from the childcare centre is, of course, a "no".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What has not been emphasised enough is the public health role that parents play.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: By taking time off to care for their symptomatic children, they keep all of us safe.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just as we should not take our essential workers for granted, we should not take parents for granted as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Fifteen months of sending symptomatic students home, of intermittent school closures, of on-and-off home-based learning.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Parents need childcare sick leave to fulfil their public and moral healthcare responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government needs to legislate for this urgently.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am calling for childcare sick leave which is backed by a medical certificate (MC), which is issued by a doctor.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We must legislate to provide our people with parent-care leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is not just the young ones who need our care.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is also the old folks, those confronting the harsh tides of ill health, unfamiliar technologies and lonely spaces.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These folks, having lived through the racial riots, the oil crisis, the Asian Financial Crisis and SARS, now face COVID-19, possibly the greatest challenge our nation has faced yet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For many, it is the straw that has broken the camel's back.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Last year, suicides rose to its highest level in 10 years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Things have gotten much harder for our lonesome elderly folks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To attend a medical appointment, they have to fumble with TraceTogether and with SafeEntry, processes that may make no intuitive sense to them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The buildings they have to pass through may have half its entrances and exits mysteriously locked.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The friendly faces on the streets whom they once asked for help are now covered by masks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is an alien world for many of our elderly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How we help our oldest citizens is not a straightforward question to answer but we know with certainty that they need care and support.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For those lucky enough to have family members who love them, we must unblock this channel of care.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government already knows parent-care leave is important.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That is why we offer it to our public servants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That is why public servants do take up such leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we need to extend this to the rest of our working adults.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Not all of us choose to bear children but all of us were born from parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For those lucky enough to still have their parents around, we need to give them the opportunity to care for them, particularly in this time of medical and social emergency.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to legislate for parent-care leave urgently.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the Resilience Budget, the Fortitude Budget and the various other supplementary Budgets, we have done a great deal to support Singaporeans and I thank the Government for that.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Out of sight and out of mind for many of us are our migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For much of the past 15 months, migrant workers in our dorms have been confined within their dorms.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For many workers, the only places they have been are literally just two places: their dorm and their worksite.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some can apply for leave to leave their dorm but I understand it is not for everyone and it is only for three hours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Three hours out of the 168 hours a week, out of their dorms or worksite.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We Singaporeans complain about the restrictions on dining-in, about how we cannot squeeze our friends into a table of five or a table of two.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the problem we face is, for many migrant workers, a distant fantasy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They have not had the chance to meet their friends.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They have not had the chance to walk free like human beings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Their basic human needs of socialisation, entertainment, physical freedom have not been met.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And remember, they, too, are worried about their loved ones back home during this pandemic, loved ones they have not seen for years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have heard heartening stories of volunteer groups that organise small group outings for migrant workers on Hippo buses with strict safe management measures in place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These ad hoc outings provide this small group of workers brief respite.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such volunteer efforts, important as they are, are only temporary relief for a very small group of migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some migrant workers even live in dorms without recreation centres.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are workers who are also tested for COVID-19 regularly and live and work under strict safe management measures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As with everything we do, there are risks involved.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we can have various measures to mitigate the risks of these plans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can do things in batches, in phases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I remember at the start of our circuit breaker, many Members of this House as well as the Government spoke with heartfelt appreciation for the sacrifices of our migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But as our voices have wound down, our migrant workers' restrictions have not.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They continue to suffer and, especially, suffer mentally.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to take concrete action in the short term and make concrete plans in the long term to ensure our migrant friends can meet their human needs of socialisation and physical freedom.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, I hope we will support those suffering by offering them something other than money.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to give childcare sick leave and parent-care leave to our working adults.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to offer safe, calibrated ways for our fully vaccinated migrant workers to meet, socialise and unwind under strict safe management measures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Time and physical freedom are things the Government has the power to offer and I hope we take urgent, concrete steps to offer them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I wish to touch on three specific issues.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, the Government should be cognisant of the current situation when deciding on increasing rental and fee charges.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We know that one group that has been badly affected is the hawkers and the market stallholders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When dining-in was suspended earlier, some hawkers faced the possibility of closing down for good.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our current dine-in restrictions affect our hawkers and their incomes significantly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is an integral part of our Singapore identity and recognised on the UNESCO Heritage List.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Hawkers offer dishes rich in local flavours at affordable prices.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is pertinent in these economically uncertain times.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government do more to help our hawkers, especially those who would really like to continue but lack the financial means to do so?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is there any ongoing effort to reach out to those on the verge of closing down and giving up their licences?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It appeared to be ill-timed and devoid of sensitivity and empathy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many members of the public spoke up on behalf of the hawkers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They expressed disappointment and dismay with the move.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The subsequent response also came across as lacking in compassion.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: NEA has made a number of exceptions in light of the pandemic, including subsidising table cleaning and dishwashing services.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could the rental revision not have waited at least until after the restrictions have been relaxed for a period of time?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A rent increase is still an increase, regardless of how small and no matter how few would be affected.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This whole episode exemplified a seeming disconnect between the public and policymakers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I hope, in future, when similar issues arise, agencies can exercise more flexibility and sensitivity when imposing rental and fee increases.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is with the aim of ensuring that such a situation does not occur again.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps the Ministries in charge of the Statutory Boards and agencies should play a stronger gatekeeping role.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They should make sure that such fee increases proposed by their agencies are approved before they are allowed to be implemented.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am glad that the focus of the Supplementary Budget is on SMEs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A significant amount of money is going to the SMEs in the form of the extended Jobs Support Scheme, rental reliefs, the extension of the Temporary Bridging Loan Programme and the Enhanced Enterprise Financing Scheme – Trade Loan.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Besides these, there are still many financing schemes under Enterprise Singapore to tap on.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is literally an alphabet soup of schemes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There are 10 grants alone under Enterprise Singapore and this does not include loans, tax incentives, investments, mentorships and so on.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Thirty-nine percent are even expecting to cut manpower.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is a shame that there is such a huge wealth of resources to support our local businesses and yet they are not put to use.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Businesses' feedback is that there are simply too many schemes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Businesses are, hence, not sure how or which one they are eligible for.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Has the Government done further analysis and engaged our SMEs to find out why the businesses are not participating?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the schemes be further streamlined and repackaged so that companies do not have to deal with multiple applications for different schemes?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can we match eligible businesses to the right schemes and connect with these businesses to provide the necessary advice?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One solution is for the SME support to be delivered as packages instead of in a modular format today.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The packages can be tailored for specific industries.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The application process should also be digitalised end-to-end and be a seamless click through.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In doing so, there might be a need to not only adjust the generosity of the packages but to simplify the packages that will enable and incentivise more SME businesses to get access to the support.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Even as we look forward to a full re-opening of the economy, the Government will continue to incur many expenses to keep our businesses and individuals abreast with the evolving pandemic situation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We are currently having the largest Budget deficit in our history despite the best efforts to manage the Budget judiciously.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: All these points to an impetus to bring forward the imminent GST hike, which is scheduled to be implemented between 2022 and 2025.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Nobody likes to pay increased prices, especially in this climate.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Even the traditional arguments for hiking GST and then providing rebates to the people worst affected may not be salient in a crisis like today.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If there is a need to raise money, perhaps the Government should consider raising other taxes within reason.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This could be more acceptable to the general public once the economy stabilises.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Government should be more flexible and sensitive when imposing rental and fee increases, including the GST hike.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In my Budget Debate speech, I spoke on how Singapore can lead the way in climate change in our own way, taking into account our strengths and our constraints.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Since then, the climate change space has only intensified, with companies facing ratcheting pressure not only from climate activists, but also from investors, governments and citizens, especially the youths.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It also deemed Shell responsible for emissions from its customers and suppliers, what we call Scope 3 emissions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The ruling also frames Shell's activities as a violation of the human rights of the citizens of the Netherlands.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The ramifications could be far-reaching for the fossil fuel industry, as well as the countries for whom the industry makes up a significant portion of their GDP, including Singapore.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As we continue to manage COVID-19 as a society, we must fundamentally prioritise climate and sustainability to build back better.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The best COVID-19 recovery plans will fight climate change, too.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And so, I was glad to hear the Minister reaffirm our commitment to invest in a green and sustainable future even while budgets are reallocated to extend more support measures for Phase Two (Heightened Alert).

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has made bold commitments to climate ambitions in Green Plan 2030.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Minister Grace Fu has recently detailed plans on how the public sector will lead the way in areas like energy, waste, transport and infrastructure, to reach peak carbon emissions around 2025, five years ahead of the broader economy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Alongside commitments and policies, we have the opportunity to stimulate green growth with infrastructure investments and support for climate solution innovations, that is, investment in new technologies and enablement of new business models and markets as core tools.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As we think about recovery, let us all ask ourselves if we have done all we can to accelerate those areas of climate mitigation that maximise speed and impact, such as the expansion of public transport, deployment of large-scale renewables, such as solar energy, building retrofits, expansion of the energy grid, including EV charging points, incentives for improving industrial efficiency and the scale-up of carbon capture, utilisation and storage.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There are many quick wins: reducing emissions through low-cost or mature technologies that typically also generate savings.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, I urge the Government to prioritise and not delay on projects with climate-change impact for want of money or manpower.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And for projects that have been delayed by COVID-19, these actually give us an opportunity to accelerate some transitions now.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Take the delays we have seen in housing projects.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: You see, a few years ago, in the HIP plan, they were asked to vote on L-shaped CDRs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But in the meantime, newer retractable CDRs came on the market.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Since there was a delay, my residents asked, "Why can't we get the latest?" In this case, the answer given to us was that the stock had already been purchased and that was what the residents had voted on.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Of course, they had not been offered retractable CDRs to vote on back then.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: While CDRs may appear trivial for some, there are parallels to climate-change solutions in housing.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: HDB is already testing and implementing multiple initiatives for more sustainable towns, such as solar and smart LED.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: More ambitious moves are being implemented, such as the centralised cooling system in Tengah eco-town, where the district level scale gives the required economies of scale.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These projects actually put us ahead of many other countries.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As we work through the backlog of new builds and improvement projects, I hope we will take the opportunity to consider if some changes ought to be made to the original plans to accelerate the conversion of every town to an eco-town, to leapfrog.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And that, as an adviser, I will soon see in the NRP and HIP proposals not just new playgrounds and new toilets, but also new coatings and new energy-efficient kitchens and other appliances offered as options.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Done at scale, it could pay for itself.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The technologies already exist in housing and in other sectors.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For more costly levers and investments, let us accelerate efforts to support the growth of financing that mitigates climate risks, as well as the growth of the market for green bonds for sure and also transition financing and other tools that will be needed to realise the goals of the Paris Agreement.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Let us collaborate in ecosystems – companies, investors, Government and Universities and research institutions – to accelerate the speed and scale of change and overcome traditional barriers via collaboration and risk sharing.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Whether it is petrochemicals, transport or shipping, an ecosystem approach is necessary, as well as a mindset shift.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We need to start looking at companies not only as sources of emissions, but as providers of climate solutions that create business values.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Companies must see the business opportunity in climate action.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In his speech on 5 July, Minister Lawrence Wong addressed how the Government was looking to support the population through the outbreak, namely, addressing the measures to take care of the health of the population and the financial support provided to individuals.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The various Ministerial Statements yesterday have been reassuring in answering some of the concerns I had over recent developments.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: However, as we consider and debate the health of the economy, as a healthcare professional myself, I want to talk about the health of society.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I am talking about physical health, mental health and emotional health.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In this pandemic, I do not deny that the physical health of the people is a priority and we want to ensure that Singapore, to the best that we can, is COVID-19-safe as we push for greater vaccination rates.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, there might be better ways we can ensure that the society is safe, without measures being overly taxing on the people.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Rostered Routine Testing (RRT) that has been implemented is an extremely resource-intensive task.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As we debate on the financial support being spent to help affected individuals and companies, we should also ask: has our spending to ensure that the population is safe been effective?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: This is an invasive, deep nasal swab that has been performed on construction, marine, maritime, manufacturing and migrant workers residing in dormitories on a regular basis since mid-2020, recently, implemented on inpatient healthcare workers.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Inpatients and visitors also do a less invasive nose swab – the Antigen Rapid Test (ART) – before they are allowed entry to hospitals.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The costs are not only financial, but to the health of these people.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The professional bodies may be able to assist in such a survey.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Deep nasal swabs should perhaps be used as the gold standard diagnostic test for the high-risk in a population, namely, identified potential clusters rather than be used for baseline screening in RRT.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: With promising developments of less invasive methods being used for testing, notably the saliva-based tests, breathalysers which some of you have tried out before the Parliament Sitting yesterday, I wonder if the implementation of RRT could be revised to include these less invasive but adequately effective testing methods.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: While the Ministries have worked hard to ensure that everyone is physically safe, it comes at the cost of mental health.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: At the national level, I believe this manifest as the fabric of society.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: We see it last week, as we shifted back into Phase Two (Heightened Alert).

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As a nation, we just inched out of our shell, only to scoot backwards hurriedly.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Not being able to dine in, not being able to meet people face to face, it takes a toll on the mental health of our people.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: What I see is the hurt from these people.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot deny that we must stay safe to protect our loved ones.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: But we also cannot deny the strain that the pandemic has put on us, whether physically, emotionally, financially and our inability to reach out to connect with others.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: It will soon be reaching two long years in our battle against the pandemic.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: We need to be able to support one another, especially to destigmatise mental illness and channel more support towards avenues where people can reach out and ask for help for their mental health.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The MTF described a future where Singapore would be in endemic mode on 24 June – but it has been a month and here we are, managing the virus in pandemic mode.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: With sudden changes, a lot of back and forth in the measures, with no sight of whether things can get better or how decisions are made, sometimes it feels like we are always having to shift and having to suffer.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Money is only a stopgap to some of the issues we face.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Grants can only do so much to help businesses recoup their losses, or for people to regain their jobs and their dignity.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: We need to find a new, sustainable balance between preventing risks to our physical health and preserving the delicate fabric that holds our society and our economy together.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: We need to take control of how we take and manage risks.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: While the vaccination target is a good one to have, it is not clear if we will shift out of Phase Two (Heightened Alert) once it has been hit.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The pandemic is uncertain, but citizens will benefit if milestones have been set and we keep to them.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: We need the Government to be able to trust us to do the right thing.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: No one wants to be the one responsible for the next outbreak.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The so-called KTV cluster: what exactly happened at these places?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Do the patrons and hostesses understand how COVID-19 is spread?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Is there a medical indication to perform urethral, vaginal and anal swabs to look for viral shedding?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: At the fish port and wet markets, likewise, what is the root cause of the spread?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Could it be a simple barrier breach because their masks got wet?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: By understanding the route of transmission, only then can we educate each other on how to minimise risks.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: These are some of the basic safe tips I know: wear a dry surgical mask; practise good hand hygiene; do not touch your face; keep a physical distance.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As much as health and safety is of utmost importance, the body is not the only thing we have.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Let us work together to create a healthy and happy Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Several Members have asked about COVID-19-related management measures.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, we had an extensive discussion on this yesterday.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, I do not really want to add much to this.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But I do want to address briefly points made by several Members about the abrupt and sudden changes that we had all had to experience these past few weeks.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I thought we had explained it yesterday but I think it worth repeating.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: From the start of this pandemic, we have been upfront, transparent with Singaporeans about the challenges we face, about our assessment of the situation and sought to communicate that as best as we can.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Obviously, it is very hard to predict what will happen.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We do not even know what will happen in the next few days, let alone the next few weeks or months.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, everyone needs to understand that we are operating in a highly fluid, rapidly changing and very uncertain environment.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Just think about this: in the lead-up to where we are today, in early July, what were the cases like?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: On 11 July, zero cases for the first time in quite a long while.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Any risk dashboard would tell you things are okay and we would be able to move forward to open confidently.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: No warning, no early indicator, but it struck us.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But based on our assessment of the KTV cluster then, we felt it was still possible to proceed but, perhaps, slow down the pace of opening.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And, therefore, we put in place the "five, two rule" which we talked about yesterday.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But shortly after that, we had the Jurong Fishery Port cluster and our assessment of that cluster was that this was much, much more serious.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The cases were already in the community through our markets, our hawker centres.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There was heightened risk of exponential spread and our vaccination coverage at that time was not adequate.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is why we decided at that time that we had to return to Phase Two (Heightened Alert).

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I think if you look at the facts today, I am fully convinced that that was the right judgement call.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is about four times the size of the KTV cluster and it is still growing.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If we had not done the Heightened Alert, the outcomes would have been far worse.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Remember we still have 200,000 seniors above 60 who are not vaccinated.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Are we prepared to live with an outcome where many of them fall sick and even succumb to the illness?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Is that something we want to see happen in Singapore?

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I know everyone is frustrated about the measures.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The minute I announce something, I get it in my inbox already.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But I hope Members in this House understand, too.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have tried very hard to explain to all of you in the hope that you, too, understand what an important, difficult but necessary decision this has to be, so that you, too, can do your part as responsible Members of Parliament in a crisis and pandemic like this, to explain to your residents, to your constituents, who, yes, I understand, are frustrated, are upset; explain why we had to do this – difficult but necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And as I said yesterday, we will monitor the situation.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We know that hospitalisation and ICU cases happen with a lag.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we will see what happens in the next few days with the ICU cases and the cases of those who are severely ill.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will look at and see if we can continue to keep the cases under control.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Then, I mentioned the next milestone comes in September when we will reach 80% of people in Singapore receiving two doses and, hopefully, similar coverage for our seniors aged 70 and above, then we can make the next move of easing.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, that is already revealing some sense of what roadmap one can expect.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is not all the details because we are still fleshing out details around specific measures and, potentially, next steps after September.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And as I have said, when we are ready, when we have more information, we will certainly share this with Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Recognising that as we open up with a higher vaccination coverage, our focus will change and we will shift our focus, not just looking at daily infection cases but paying more attention to those who are hospitalised and in ICU.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Based on that shift, hopefully then, if we see more cases emerging as we open, we can have some confidence.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So long as hospitalisation and ICU cases remain stable, we can have some confidence that we, hopefully, will not have to go back to Heightened Alert again.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As I have said, important qualifier; so long as hospitalisation and ICU cases remain stable and at an acceptable level.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we know that we cannot rule out things from worsening.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We know that we cannot rule out the risk of new variants coming, that you may have a more severe outbreak, more people hospitalised and, therefore, we have to be prepared we may have to put in additional restrictions down the road; hopefully, not like what we had gone through over these past few weeks and months.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But that is the uncertainty that we all have to face and we all should face it together, recognising that this is something we all have to deal with during this pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I would certainly not like to have to impose restrictions again, if I can help it.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But if the situation worsens to such an extent where hospitalisation and ICU cases go up, I think, despite our high vaccination coverage, perhaps because of a new variant, then we will have to understand these are the risks and why we may have to put in place such measures.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, I hope this explanation will give everyone a better sense of understanding, appreciation, of why we did what we did and what to expect.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have shared as much as we can up to now.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And as I have said, when further details are ready, we will share more.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many of you also have suggestions on other COVID-19-related measures that you think might be adjusted and I want to assure you that the MTF will continue to study all these suggestions carefully, as we review and update our strategies.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Several Members offered suggestions in other areas like childcare leave and workplace fairness.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These will require careful study by the relevant Ministries and will be considered and addressed on other occasions.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, I do not propose to dwell too much on them.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In my response today, I would like to touch on two broad areas that Members have raised.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, how we are helping workers and businesses to ride through this period of Heightened Alert.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Second, how we are preparing for the next phase and gearing up for a post-pandemic world.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Based on the amount available for spending, we then had to carefully design the measures to meet the needs of businesses and workers who are most affected.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We also took into consideration the strong base of existing measures that have already been rolled out in previous Budgets and which are still in place today.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They include the Wage Credit Scheme which continues to support businesses which provided wage increases to their Singaporean workers.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The SMEs Go Digital programme and the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package, all of these schemes, programmes, measures, already part of the baseline, part of the existing support and the vast majority of the support, in fact, go to SMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There is also existing support for specific areas like the arts and sports sectors, which Mr Sharael Taha, Mr Mark Chay and Ms Raeesah Khan spoke about.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, sports coaches and fitness instructors can benefit from the Continuing Coach Education Training Allowance and the Self-Employed Person (SEP) Project Grant.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Likewise, we have similar support schemes for arts and culture, freelancers and organisations.

speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
